#4290. Battlefield 6’s first big map in months is coming to Labs soon, but I'm more excited about BF4's Golmud Railway making its way to BF6

As promised, Battlefield Labs is coming back to bring us a preview of some of Battlefield 6’s upcoming Season 2 content.

Battlefield 6’s Season 2 was recently pushed back by a month to give Battlefield Studios time to polish up its content. Now, the developer has revealed how it plans to use some of that time, and the first port of call is Battlefield Labs.

As discussed in the initial delay message, BF Studios wants the community’s involvement earlier and more consistently in the development of future content. This includes Season 2, of course, and a big component of what it’s bringing to the game is headed to Labs.

The first Battlefield Labs session kicking off soon will focus on Contaminated, one of the new maps coming to Battlefield 6 with Season 2. BF Studios says the map falls between Eastwood and Mirak Valley, in terms of size.

The blog post even likened it to Battlefield 1’s St. Quentin Scar, and Battlefield 5’s Arras. Although we’ve yet to actually play it, the size and description do sound really well, especially in a game as starved of big maps as Battlefield 6 currently is.

Another thing BF Studios wants to test is the way ground vehicle gameplay and aerial presence interact with infantry combat, which is pretty standard for most Battlefield maps. Interestingly, there appears to be some sort of mechanic unique to Contaminated that the developer also wants to evaluate.

More Labs sessions are planned, including one that will show off new gameplay tools and vehicles. The AH-6 Little Bird helicopter was specifically namedropped, which makes sense given that it’s going to be part of Season 2’s content.

Battlefield Labs sessions will also extend beyond the biggest-ticket items of maps and vehicles. BF Studios said we should expect tests of upcoming features, like the Aircraft Radar, as part of a list of other air combat updates.

Ground vehicles, and they way the various rockets interact with them, will also be evaluated in a different session, with specific adjustments planned for RPGs and TOWs. And, of course, the work to improve and perfect hit reg remains ongoing, and future tweaks will go through Labs first.

There’s even more exciting news for fans of big maps, as the blog post also confirmed that Battlefield 4’s Golmud Railway is currently in the works, planned to go live in a future season. Golmud Railway will show up early in Labs, and you can expect it to evolve over multiple sessions.

For context, when it does arrive in Battlefield 6, Golmud Railway will be the largest map in the game, which is saying something. Though the map is beloved by vehicle players, it has its issues elsewhere, and BF Studios says it will be looking at all that when it creates the BF6, emphasising that it won’t be a simple port of the BF4 original.

Finally, the post throws a bone to Redsec battle royale players still waiting for a Solo mode. BF Studios continues to test the idea internally, but it’s taking a while. Needless to say, there are so many aspects that need to be considered. Game pace, balance, player survivability, match flow just to name a few.

Redsec BR was built with squads in mind, so that task is extra challenging. Though the developer didn’t say when we can expect Solos to arrive in Labs, players will get a chance to experience it before it enters the live game.

#4288. Remedy Explains Control Resonant's Most Memorable, Unexpected Sequence And Its [REDACTED] Inspirations

Please allow the first sentence here to warn you that this interview discusses a portion of Control Resonant that takes place near the end of the game and is arguably the most unexpected and surprising sequence. I encourage you to experience it without spoilers. So if you haven't beaten the game yet, please do, and then come back to this page.However, if you have beaten the game, or curiosity has driven you to learn what game has been redacted from the headline and why (it's the 1995 Super Nintendo RPG, EarthBound, by the way), then please read on.

In the late-game of Control Resonant – basically right before you tackle the final confrontation – the game suddenly shifts timeframe and genre to become a 16-bit RPG. The nostalgic lens turns the game into something that feels like 1995's EarthBound, complete with turn-based battles, in order to explain the trauma that Jesse and Dylan went through at a young age after they came across an object of power: the slide projector. The whole sequence is funny, heartbreaking, weird, and importantly effective at making you feel you are seeing a part of their past. It was particularly effective on me as I have fond memories of playing EarthBound and games like it when I was young. To see and experience Dylan and Jesse's childhood this way felt accurate, as absurd as that sounds.

I reached out to Remedy to specifically discuss that portion of the game. You can find the full e-mail interview below with the team members who contributed to its creation.

The big RPG backstory sequence for Jesse and Dylan – why approach the storytelling that way?

Lead level designer, Anne-Marie Grönroos: The basis for the whole sequence is that the Hedron attacks Dylan's mind, breaks his reality apart, and he has to rebuild himself. We wanted the reality-breaking part to affect the game itself and have the player feel some of the confusion Dylan is feeling by breaking the fourth wall.

Who pitched that sequence, how did they pitch it, and was it difficult to sell to the larger team?

Grönroos: At Remedy, ideas rarely come from a single person or team, and we rarely do formal pitches, but rather discuss and workshop ideas cross-craft until they start taking the shape of something we like. The initial idea from the writer was for this to be a text-based adventure, to return to a very early form of a video game to show that the Patterning is devolving him, but an Alan Wake 2 DLC had already done that, and we wanted to find something else.

Independently, some months ago a level designer had suggested a sidequest with JRPG pixel graphics, but that had gone nowhere. I remembered that and suggested doing an old Final Fantasy-style JRPG here, which also felt more fitting since that’s the type of game Dylan and Jesse would have played in their childhood, and not a text-based adventure. People got excited about that, and after some concerns about feasibility, we went forth with it. It helped that the level designer who had originally wanted to do the JRPG side quest is a big fan of these types of games and has made them before. I wouldn’t have dropped something this crazy on someone who wasn’t passionate about it and ready to figure out how to do it with our engine that’s not built for anything like this.

Is EarthBound (Mother in Japan) the primary inspiration for that sequence? Are there big fans of those games at Remedy?

Senior level designer in charge of the JRPG quest, Arhi Makkonen:The whole Quest was born from that childhood feeling I had when playing old JRPGs – Final Fantasy, Breath of Fire, Chrono Trigger, Secret of Mana, Bahamut Lagoon, and yes, Mother. The most important thing for me was capturing that feeling of a time when games felt like magic. I think many people can relate to that nostalgia, and now Jesse and Dylan share that feeling in the game.Visually, Mother was a major inspiration of course. Juuso Anttila is the concept artist who did all the splendid pixel art for Rebuild quest. Mother's style fits the mysterious Americana small town vibe perfectly. We also couldn't pass up the pun about a story revolving around "Not-Mother" that was made in the style of Mother.

Was it difficult to implement the sequence into the game? Did Remedy's Northlight Engine need significant work to account for the sequence?

Makkonen: The Northlight engine was designed to work perfectly for third-person action games. Well, Rebuild Quest is pretty much the opposite of that. Northlight is a specialized tool rather than a general-purpose one, so we had to come up with some rather creative solutions to create a 2D JRPG.

First of all, we’re faking the 2D look. In reality, the entire JRPG Ordinary exists within a 3D world that the camera simply views from directly overhead. It occupies a tiny patch in a remote corner of the game world—a space where 3D Dylan would barely have room to stand. The entire game-within-a-game is written in Lua; our incredibly versatile game designer, Tommi Saalasti, created the underlying system, upon which I was then able to build the story.

Since we didn't really have the tools to create a game like this, I had to hand-code every single detail. Dylan takes one step up, Dylan turns left (where Jesse hopefully is at that moment), text box 1, text box 2. The Lua script for the Rebuild quest alone probably contains as many lines of code as all the other quests in the game combined. And then there were things like animations were restricted to a maximum of two frames, and some UI elements were created using static particle effects.

So yes, we faced all sorts of challenges and compromises, but at the heart of it all was a wonderful story – simply told in a somewhat unconventional way. We trusted that the narrative would make up for some of the imperfections.

Remedy has a reputation for big unexpected and often crazy singular moments. What are the conversations like around delivering those? In pre-production, are there conversations like, "What is the big moment for this one?" Or do they happen pretty naturally?

Grönroos: They both happen naturally and we also have conversations about what the big moments should be. Sometimes we like a section so much that we decide to put even more resources and importance to it, even if it wasn’t supposed to be all that important from the get-go. The Into the Sinkhole quest, for instance, is a quest that wasn’t planned to be a “tentpole moment” from the start, but we kept putting more effort into it when it was shaping up to be something very special.

But most setpieces in the game were planned to be such from the early stages of pre-production. In Resonant, we wanted to have multiple standout moments instead of a single sequence like the Ashtray Maze overshadowing everything else, and I’m happy to see that players have different favorites.

And a different approach from Control is that several of these memorable moments (Sinkhole, Underpass Fault, the JRPG section) are more emotional and subdued instead of bombastic action (although we also have big action setpieces), which was an interesting challenge itself.

Was there a fear that the visuals would limit the emotional impact of the sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, but we decided to trust the writing. Several other games have managed to deliver a similar emotional impact despite pixel graphics (and sometimes because of them, since the level [of] abstraction can make characters more relatable and up to the player’s interpretation), so we weren’t too concerned.

Was there a fear that action game fans would be frustrated by the RPG sequence?

Grönroos: Yes, this was the main concern about the sequence. It was a very polarizing sequence in the playtests: people either loved or hated it. We did discuss shortening it significantly, but in the end decided to keep it as it is but added some fast travel options and make some parts skippable. There were more fans than haters, and we didn’t want to sacrifice something we really enjoyed.

How concerned were you about the actual RPG mechanics of that sequence?

Makkonen: Since Rebuild doesn't feature a vast number of battles, we didn't need to build particularly deep RPG or progression systems. The combat served as an additional storytelling tool – illustrating how bullies torment Dylan, showing his first fight (against rats, naturally), and depicting his eventual abduction by the FBC.

Refining the combat to be simple, yet offer the player meaningful choices required a few iterations. In addition to standard attacks, the children can occasionally use special abilities: Dylan delivers a heavy blow to a single enemy, while Jesse fires at everyone. Enemies deal enough damage that defending becomes necessary when multiple foes target the same character.

The lightbulbs in The Underpass mission goes in similarly unexpected, animated directions. How did that mission come about? What was the pitch like for that one?

Grönroos: That one started with the idea of doing something comically mundane, switching lightbulbs, and adding a paranatural twist to it. The cartoon man wasn’t in the initial version, but instead we were going to do live action videos and have Dylan get stuck in that video as the end twist. They were supposed to be old-fashioned “work safety” videos explaining how to change lightbulbs, and as the quest went on, it became more and more obvious that the maintenance guy in the videos was too aware of what Dylan was doing. This all came out from a one-hour workshop.

There wasn’t really a pitch, but rather a back-and-forth like “could we do a quest about Dylan changing lightbulbs in a ritualistic way? We could have these sentient work safety videos explain how to do it and “Dylan could get trapped inside the video.” Much later, when the live action turned out to be a no-go, we pivoted to the current cartoon instead, and that was even funnier than our initial idea.

#4286. Arc Raiders finally reveals early 2026 roadmap, but we’re not getting a new map for a while

The first couple of months of 2026 in the world of Arc Raiders look pretty promising, but the big guns are being held back for now.

After weeks of waiting, Arc Raiders developer Embark has officially unveiled the first few months of the game’s 2026 roadmap. The plan is split into four months, covering January to April, collectively dubbed Escalation.

We’re expecting a content update each month, with the majority of the biggest additions happening on the game’s existing maps. There is, however, at least one new map in the works, but it won’t be here until sometime in April.

While we wait for that, Arc Raiders is going to go through several events and other in-game changes, some more meaningful (and exciting) than others. January looks to be the lightest so far, which makes sense given that it’s just a week or so from ending.

January’s chapter is titled Headwinds, kicking off on January 27. This segment will see the addition of a new matchmaking option for players above level 40 - at or near the game’s endgame. We’re also expecting a new Map Condition, and a new Player Project for everyone to contribute to.

Things start getting interesting in February, when Shrouded Sky will begin. This chapter brings three exciting additions to Arc Raiders. There will be a new Map Condition, new Arc Threat, and the start of another Player Project.

Interestingly, we’re going to see some sort of map update during the month, but Embark didn’t share anymore details. The next Raider Deck will also deploy in February, alongside a new Expedition Window.

The Flashpoint chapter begins in March, when we’re expecting another new Map Condition, one more new Arc Threat, as well as another Player Project. March’s most interesting addition is an update to everyone’s trusty rooster friend, Scrappy.

Finally, April is when the big guns come out, because that’s when the first new map of 2026 will arrive in Arc Raiders. With it, comes a new large Arc, which is to be expected. A new Map Condition will debut then, too, likely starting off on the new map.

That’s pretty much it, but seeing as we’re just one day away from the start of the January stage, things are about to get exciting again in Arc Raiders.

#4284. God of War: Laufey has Been Delayed for Additional Polishing

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

February 2027 is set to be a massive release window, with remakes and new releases of all kinds of major series hitting one after another. Because of this, a few titles have pushed their release dates back, opting instead to give February releases their time and allowing gamers' wallets a bit of time to recover.

Wuthering Waves is one of the biggest Gachas on the planet, and they do far better than most at answering player complaints. Let's go over exactly how!

Santa Monica Studio joins the teams leaning away from February 2027, as the previously planned God of War: Laufey has been delayed to May 20th, 2027. With how important Laufey’s individual performance needs to be, Santa Monica Studio is making the most of the time they have, refusing to fall for the age-old pull of rushing release in order to present the best game possible.

Santa Monica Studio is easily one of the most prestigious teams under Sony, releasing banger after banger with the God of War series. Coming off the announcement of remakes of the original trilogy, Santa Monica revealed a major gamble with God of War Laufey, the first title in the franchise without Kratos as the central playable character.

The game focuses on Kratos’ wife and Atreus’s mother, Laufey, one of the last Norse giants present in the new God of War’s setting. Trapped within a mystical realm of the afterlife, Laufey seems to be taking major notes from the PS2/PS3 God of War titles, pitting its protagonist against a truly magical set of foes with only one way out.

After some of the more grounded presentation and general combat of the last two God of War titles, Laufey seems like a perfect return to form, one that the team is making sure hits as hard as possible. The release date change is disappointing for eager fans, but it does wonders to dodge some other heavy hitters dropping in February.

If Laufey stuck to its original release plan, the game would be battling titans like Fable, Persona 4 Revival, and Metro 2039, all major releases gamers are setting aside cash and time for. Not that God of War Laufey wouldn’t be able to hang, but it's worth taking a step back if the team could afford to.

Being one of Sony’s flagship studios doesn’t mean that Santa Monica is free of danger, if their recent treatment of Suckerpunch is any indication, but ensuring a good release is best both for the team and the consumers. Laufey doesn’t have the immediate pull for long-time players who haven’t kept up with the new God of War titles, so it needs to stand on its own as strongly as possible.

Santa Monica is a team known for absolute polish, and their refusal to be rushed is a great sign that maintaining this quality is a top priority. Too many games have been released in recent years only to be cannibalized by post-launch patches that add functions that should already be there, a mistake Santa Monica Studio is being careful to avoid.

After some of the more grounded presentation and general combat of the last two God of War titles, Laufey seems like a perfect return to form, one that the team is making sure hits as hard as possible.

May is also a much cushier release month in terms of competing releases, with no major drops ready to clash with God of War Laufey’s acclaim. The new title by Santa Monica Studio may feel like a spinoff meant to buy time, but the opportunity to learn more about Laufey, such an impactful character in the new God of War series, is incredibly exciting for any fans of that saga.

Finally getting her side of the story is a phenomenal way of closing the saga for now, allowing Kratos to rest on his laurels while expanding the wildly fantastical side of not only the Norse saga, but the entire worldwide mythos of God of War.

Despite some early concerns that Phantom Blade Zero would be easy, it's not. Players have flocked to certain corners of the internet to express which enemies are giving them trouble, and things have gotten so bad that the developer, S-Game, has already had to nerf one boss, with more expected.

If waiting for nerfs isn't your style, or you're stuck and can't move on, one player has you covered. They've created a complete cheat menu with auto-parry, auto-block, and unlimited consumables.

A few games have received cheat menus over the last few weeks. One came to Baldur's Gate 3 on console in September, and last month, The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered got one. Now it's Phantom Blade Zero's turn.

This menu comes with over 15 cheats, each one designed to make the game that little bit easier (or harder) for you. It includes cheats to buff your Sha-Chi, spawn rare items, and multiply the damage you deal. The full list of cheats can be found below:

Unfortunately, the cheat menu is only available on PC and can be downloaded and installed from Nexus Mods.

While this menu makes things easier, others are doing their best to make Phantom Blade Zero harder. One creator has turned the game into a full Soulslike experience, adding respawning enemies, Remnant Dust you can lose, and bosses that return to their original phase. The same creator also created content that makes normal attacks and dodges cost Sha-Chi, as well as a Boss Rush mode.

If you're reluctant to use a cheat menu, we've got you covered. We've created guides for the game's best weapons, best Phantom Edges, best accessories, and best builds. Using these could be the push you need to get you over the line.

#4281. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 23, 2026

This week has been home to some disheartening news. BioWare, the creators of games like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, is being shut down amid a flurry of layoffs. It's another frustrating story from a struggling video game industry. Below you will find some of our stories about the legendary developer, including our massive 2016 oral history. And then after that, you can read about our recommendations of what to play this weekend.

I spent the early hours playing Final Fantasy Resonance trying to figure out precisely why I couldn't put it down. I eventually realized that the game manages in a very purposeful way to answer that quiet need I've so frequently had: "I wish I could experience a game just like Final Fantasy IV or VI again, for the first time, but with a new cast and story." That's pretty much what you can expect here; Resonance is a very purposeful throwback experience that harkens to the early days of FF pixel adventures, but with several modern conveniences, graphical flourishes, and depth added into the mix. It's a big and refreshingly wholesome journey of entertaining party members, summoning giant creatures, flying an airship across the world, and fighting turn-based battles that include absurd spell effects. It's one of my favorite games of the year, and well worth the time it will take to explore. Read our full review for more.

Expect to hear a lot of people proclaiming this as "one of the good ones," as Modern Warfare came out swinging this week with a strong campaign, compelling additions to competitive multiplayer, and an impressive extraction shooter mode in the form of DMZ. I've already been impressed by the first few hours of the campaign, which offers a tense, harrowing, and often disturbingly brutal story that bounces between a number of character perspectives. The gunplay feels tuned in, the traversal and melee is satisfying, and the narrative beats grounded in excellent actin performances. Our reviewer has spent even more time with the full game, and can share their full perspective to help inform whether you want to take a dive into this year's installment.

The Nintendo Sports franchise, which began with Wii Sports in 2006, has never been about the single-player experience. That remains true 20 years later in Nintendo Switch Sports Resort. But this time around, Nintendo has boosted the amount of content beyond what the series has typically provided, appealing to all player counts, all while retaining its trademark approachability. Whether you're joining together with three friends for some friendly competition across the package's 12 sports or you're trying to climb the Island Crown ladder by beating increasingly difficult single-player opponents, Switch Sports Resort is a great motion-controlled collection.

Halloween is around the corner. As you’re buying overpriced candy, deciding which version of the Joker to dress up as, and debating between watching Obsession and Backrooms over a cup of cider, it’s the perfect time to replay old horror games or dive into new ones. 2026 has a solid roster of choices for the latter thanks to releases like Resident Evil Requiem, Paranormasight: The Mermaid’s Curse, and Silent Hill: Townfall, but Tenebris Somnia shouldn’t be overlooked if you’re looking for a cool indie throwback.

Part retro-inspired adventure game, part live-action indie horror film, you’ll uncover the mystery of a nightmare-induced apartment building and battle horrors to rescue your trapped ex. The gameplay is survival horror 101, but it’s executed well, with consistently clever and inventive puzzle-solving as a highlight. It may not be a graphical powerhouse, but Tenebris Somnia still maintains a creepy atmosphere thanks to solid scares partly delivered by effective and well-made live-action cinematics. If you’re going to binge horror films, you may as well play one too. You can read my full review here.

Full disclosure: I have not played One Piece: Grand Gourmet. I was trying to finish up Castlevania: Belmont's Curse when a review game landed in my lap that I've had to give my full attention. That said, I have watched a lot of the One Piece anime, have a cat named Nami, and dog named Luffy.

I don't know if One Piece: Grand Gourmet is any good, but I like the premise and pixel graphics. One Piece is a very malleable franchise (which is why its live action adaptation is pretty good), so the idea of managing a restaurant as Sanji feels like it could be a very good fit. I plan on climbing aboard with all my hopes and dreams soon. And it is out now, which is good to know.

Similar to the entry above, I have not yet played Stupid Never Dies yet (there are too many video games!), but we like to use this weekly article to call out the new video games of the week. I am eager to check out Stupid Never Dies primarily because of its pop-punk soundtrack and 2000s aesthetic. I think it has the potential to be a fun, nostalgic throwback to my youth when I was learning Blink-182's "Dammit" on guitar and playing Devil May Cry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker has been out for just over seven weeks now, but I wouldn't blame you if you haven't finished it – or even started it – yet. A lot has come out! But if you need a reason to jump back in, this week's 1.1 update is a great excuse – the devs have added hundreds of bug fixes and other minor improvements, so it should run better than it ever did before. There's also an even easier difficulty mode if you want to cruise through without worrying about combat, and a new in-game potion that lets you respec all your skill points. I stalled out about halfway through (when I started playing Wolverine), but I'm planning to jump back in this weekend.

Oh, and you can pet dogs and cats now. Maybe I should have led with that.

Multiplayer physics mountain-climbing game Peak became one of the most viral co-op experiences of 2025 (I refuse to use the term friendslop), but only PC players have enjoyed its wacky shenanigans. That changed this week as Peak is now available on PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2. Either alone or, preferably, alongside up to three friends, you’ll try to ascend procedurally generated, absurdly unrealistic mountains riddled with dangers. Working together is key, a tricky prospect thanks to the in-game proximity chat that necessitates sticking together, but griefing each other, intentionally or otherwise, is just as entertaining – maddeningly frustrating at times, but entertaining. Peak on consoles includes all post-launch content and, best of all, supports crossplay for all platforms.

The original Azul remains one of my all-time favorite games even after many years, but it just misses the bar with its strategic complexity to be one I'd pull out to play with the kids. That why I was especially delighted to find that Azul Kids is one of those rare "adapted for children" projects that turned out extremely well.

Players take on the roll of creative young artists building mosaic displays with various colored tiles. The concept remains simple enough to work for even very young players of age five or six, but the whole family should have fun with the approachable strategy implications of choosing tiles and completing your masterpiece.

#4280. Monsta brings a turn-based portable classic to mobile, where it's you versus mutant monsters

For many of us, the history of mobile gaming only stretches back to the first iPhone, and maybe a little further if we head back to the days of flip phones and the N-Gage. But look even further back, to when PDAs (Personal Digital Assistants) were all the craze, and you'll find examples of the primordial soup of mobile gaming, such as Monsta.

First released back in the 2000s on PalmOS devices, and now available for the modern-day iOS and Android platforms, Monsta had to tackle many hardware limitations, including slow processing speed at the time. That's what inspired developer Superverse Industries to create this turn-based tactical shooter, where it's just you and a building full of monsters to get before they get you.

You'll need to plan your moves, make use of various gadgets and weapons, and deal with monsters boasting their own distinct and deadly abilities.

And more than that, the gameplay itself has also looped round from being simplified for the purpose of dealing with limited performance, to stepping into the same trend of turn-based, roguelike(ish) games that have conquered the market recently.

All this and a who's who of artists, developers and composers from that particular slice of early 2000s Serbian game development makes Monsta a game worth checking out for its historical value, if nothing else. But with over 50 handmade levels, multiple upgrades and monsters to fight off, Monsta is worth checking out as a game on its own merits!

In the meantime, if you find yourself wanting a blast from the past like Monsta just a little more, why not check out our list of the best retro-inspired games on iOS for some choice picks?

#4279. Nioh 3’s generous demo is out now, and your progress carries over to the full game

If you’re looking for a way to check out one of the biggest releases of early 2026, Team Ninja has made it easy for you.

Nioh 3 is one of the most anticipated games of 2026, and it’s easily among the biggest releases of February. We’re a few days away from the start of that month, however, but we don’t have to wait until then to actually play Team Ninja’s next major release.

The previously announced demo has arrived, and it’s one any fan of action games should check out, especially if you missed the PlayStation-exclusive beta held last year.

Unlike previous tests, the Nioh 3 demo is available on PC and PS5, just like the main game. This is pretty new for the series, which has typically launched first on PlayStation before coming to PC months later.

The Nioh 3 demo includes a decent portion of content from the beginning of the game. It’s enough to show off the core duality mechanic, letting you switch between the Samurai and Ninja styles at will. It also includes a preview of the game’s open field level design, which makes it sit somewhere between full open world and the more linear level design of past Nioh games.

Feedback from the previous beta has been implemented into the demo (and full release), so you may see some familiar faces, as well as areas you visited before - assuming you played that one.

Another big reason why you might want to grab the Nioh 3 demo is that your progress in it will carry over to the full version. This includes the character creator, too, meaning you can spend all day perfecting your character without having to worry about missing out on playing the actual game.

The demo even supports online multiplayer for up to three players, in case you come to Nioh for co-op. If you complete the available content, you’ll earn an in-game bonus in the full version. This is something Team Ninja has done with past Nioh titles, of course.

This time, your reward is the Twin-Snake Helmet. Just make sure you complete the demo before February 15.

Nioh 3 is out February 6 on PC, and PlayStation 5.

#4278. Phantom Blade Zero Review In Progress – Shaping Up To Be One Of The Best Action Games I've Ever Played

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding achievement for the action genre. So astounding that I feel pulled to experience everything it has to offer… and that means instead of rolling credits, I’ve been busy completing story-critical side quests and more to get the most complete ending. That’s another way of saying I am enjoying this game very, very much but still need more time to render a final verdict, which is why you’re reading a review-in-progress of Phantom Blade Zero rather than a scored piece.

Though I’m not interested in guesstimating a score right now, I know it will be high because Phantom Blade Zero impresses and then some. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and I’m shocked to be writing that. This is a debut of sorts for developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile games and smaller-scale titles; it’s the team’s first triple-A release, and its first game of this kind. This studio is so clearly a dedicated student of the genre, analyzing what works here and what works there in other action greats to create something of its own. It looks forward at what action games can do, can play like, can look like, while looking back at the games before it and understanding why those games – games like Devil May Cry, Elden Ring, Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice, Bayonetta, and just about every other quality action game you can think of – continue to be ones we hold so highly. Should it stick the landing, Phantom Blade Zero will join that echelon of action pedigree.

Protagonist Soul is a quiet, mostly stoic martial arts master who prefers to let his blades (of which there are so, so many) do the talking. The Order he’s sworn his life to betrays him, and, in an effort to right wrongs, he discovers a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the blood-soaked Chinese martial underground known as Wulin. As a result, puppets, secret sects, powerful god-like creatures, monstrous beasts, and much more prowl Wulin’s various biomes. I haven’t kept count, but there are a massive number of enemies to take down, both standard mob variants and bosses, and the game stays fresh throughout. It's even fresher when you consider how many weapons you can acquire on Soul’s journey.

Every weapon is wholly unique, like picking up a new character in a fighting game, each with its own moveset and abilities. Upgrading these weapons through various tiers unlocks additional abilities, and you can even Soul Temper weapons to add one final, game-changing ability or perk. A fully upgraded weapon can have a moveset that uses the majority of buttons on your controller. You can do the same with Phantom Edges, special tide-turning weapons with limited uses (before you build up additional charges). Combined with different accessories and medicine types, Phantom Blade Zero offers hundreds, perhaps thousands, of combat kit permutations. You can play as a drunken fighter who switches between sober, tipsy, and drunken states, with his range and damage output changing as a result; you can focus on a bleed build, ripping enemies to shreds with charged attacks that utilize Soul's own HP to deal extra damage (that can then be earned back with bleed); you can use lightning, wind, fire, and ice to create elemental storms against enemies, and you can use a sword that switches between different elemental states on command as well. You can also just pound enemies to pulp with Phantom Edge fists, too. I’ve struggled to stop using these fists since acquiring them because they’re so satisfying.

Forty-plus hours into Phantom Blade Zero, it feels like I’ve played as dozens of different Souls because I've discovered so many build types. S-Game smartly pushes you to try new builds and weapons as you get them, doling out generous upgrade materials and currency; it encourages you to try everything, and the next weapon might just become your new favorite.

Finding these materials (and additional fights) is great fun, too, because Phantom Blade Zero’s various open-area biomes are a genuine joy to explore. You are always rewarded for taking the optional path, and those rewards are always worthwhile. You might find a healthy pile of upgrade materials, or a boss with a weapon you’ll fall in love with. The way buildings, alleys, caves, cliffsides, and other environmental features weave in and out of each other evokes FromSoftware’s architectural design and the subsequent shortcut “aha!” moments.

That said, Phantom Blade Zero is definitively not a Soulslike, though you’d be forgiven for assuming as much given its challenging suite of bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, which are this game’s equivalent of bonfires. However, its challenge is much more surmountable (with various difficulties and accessories to ease parry and dodge timing), and its world progression is materially different. Kill an enemy and it’s dead for good, which to my surprise, adds a sense of worldbuilding I didn’t know I wanted. Progression through this journey feels tangible because I’m actually removing traces of evil with my weapons, traces that don’t respawn when I interact with checkpoints. It’s a nice change of pace that narratively speaks to Soul’s efforts.

Along the way, countless reading materials shed light on Phantom Blade Zero’s intertwining stories, and tracking down the next memory, scroll, or book entry rewards you if you’re interested in the full picture of this Wuxia story. I’d argue the game’s story is its weakest element, but only when compared to the rest of the package. It doesn't break any new ground narratively, but it provides enough mystery and thrill to keep things moving. And while performances are great, talking to characters is still mostly just two people standing across from each other talking through a new quest. Fortunately, cutscenes pick up the slack with dramatic villains, heartfelt revelations, raw tension, and more.

Production value is high across the board, thanks to incredibly impressive animation and a beautiful rendering of this dark fantasy China. Faces are lifelike, nudging up just shy of the uncanny valley as close-ups reveal porous details, lip quivers, and more, bringing an excellent cast of Chinese performances to life. The English voice acting has its standouts, but Soul’s voice is boring, so I highly recommend the Chinese vocals.

Boss fights draw clear inspiration from Chinese cinema and boast a wondrous sense of awe and scale that only the best in the genre typically offer. There are a ton of bosses, too, with very few repeats (repeats do happen in segmented challenge trials), and it’s impressive to think back on just how many I defeated, and just how many of them delivered a unique fight. I appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases as well. There are so many bosses – nearing 100 or more if I had to guess – and having my progression saved through phases removes some of the repetition I often feel when, say, phase two of a boss continues to kill me and I have to blitz through phase one again and again before taking another stab at it.

That scale and on-screen excitement carry through almost every fight in the game, down to even the simplest mob fights, though these are starting to feel a touch repetitive as I’m barreling toward the game’s end. Soul moves like the world’s greatest martial artist, but your controller inputs make it happen. If you mash the attack button, it looks nice… but if you use each weapon’s prescribed inputs and abilities, Phantom Blade Zero delivers a level of detailed action I’ve seen in few other games. You direct the game’s action, and this lets you turn what might otherwise be just another group of fodder enemies into an electric bout of spectacle.

To say I greatly enjoy this game greatly undersells my feelings – writing this review-in-progress is frustrating because I want to get back to Phantom Blade Zero. I expect to reach credits in the coming days, so please be on the lookout for my final verdict this week.

#4277. Old School RuneScape lets you test your mettle with the introduction of Hardcore Worlds

Old School RuneScape and the whole RuneScape-verse has been going for nigh-on 20 years now, and for those looking for a challenge, there are plenty of bosses and dungeons to face. But now, even the most experienced of players can face a true trial, as today, Hardcore Worlds arrive in Old School RuneScape on all platforms, mobile included.

Hardcore Worlds function exactly as you'd expect them to, but if you're new to the concept, here's a brief explainer: In Hardcore Worlds, death is final. As in no retries, no restarts. Whether it's slow or sudden, if your character perishes, you can either discard them or transfer them to a regular server, though without the rewards or goodies available exclusively on Hardcore Worlds.

And if you're curious about stepping in and giving Hardcore Worlds a go, now's a good time! Because from today, Reaper's Raffle and World First rewards will allow you to win real-world prizes by completing tasks for the Reaper. Accomplishing tasks enters you into a raffle, with plenty of exciting goodies on offer for those who step into the Hardcore worlds.

Off the back of the Road to Restoration, it seemed as if Jagex faced a stumbling block with the community rejection of RuneScape: Reignited. But if the introduction of Hardcore Worlds is any indication, they still have plenty of crowd-pleasers up their sleeve.

Still, while Old School RuneScape is undoubtedly an exciting, storied MMORPG for many fans, there's always something new vying for the spotlight. Just take a look at our list of the best mobile games of 2026 (so far) for some of our choice picks!

#4276. Report: Ghost Of Yōtei Developer Sucker Punch Hit With Layoffs

Sucker Punch, the team behind Ghost of Yōtei, Ghost of Tsushima, Infamous, and Sly Cooper, has been hit with layoffs, according to a report by Aftermath. The outlet states that 26 roles have been affected as the studio prepares its next project.

Aftermath cites a former Sucker Punch employee who confirmed the number of layoffs. The outlet also obtained a company email announcing the staff cuts.

“After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. Several positions across Sucker Punch will be eliminated as a result,” reads a section of the email. Sucker Punch then says it will work to support affected staff in their transition and will share more details next week about what comes next. The studio has not yet publicly commented on the layoffs.

This news comes a few weeks after the release of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, which originally launched in 2025 to critical and commercial success. The release coincided with the arrival of two substantial DLCs: the story expansion Echoes of Sekigahara and a roguelike mode called Most Wanted that reintroduces Ghost of Tsushima hero Jin Sakai as a playable character.

#4275. The Legacy and Evolution of Rockstar Games: How One Studio Redefined Open-World Gaming

Usama Mehmood is a Senior Writer at DualShockers with more than five years of experience in the video game industry. He has been writing professionally since 2021 and covering games since 2022, with work spanning guides, lists, reviews, and features across action-adventure games, JRPGs, open-world titles, racing games,

I grew up with an unhealthy obsession with the Grand Theft Auto series. The game wasn’t obviously meant for an 8-year-old, but it showed me the greatest gift: my parents wanting to give me happiness and comfort throughout my upbringing, even if it meant unknowingly handing me a game that was clearly meant for older audiences.

But hey, it didn’t meddle with my behavior, alright? Playing San Andreas was one of my most endearing experiences, with countless playthroughs/save files. And I mean, some of my best video game memories even involved my dad helping me clear a couple of tough missions in both it and Vice City. So from those 3D-era entries to see how far Rockstar has come to be this industry powerhouse with their sandbox video game series is genuinely astounding to see.

Aaron Garbut, co-studio head of Rockstar North, explained that no single person has the entire game mapped out in their head.

Rockstar Games has spent decades building some of the most recognisable worlds in video game history. Whether it's the streets of Los Santos, the mob-boss-riddled underworld of Liberty City, or a quiet ride through the unforgiving American frontier with an on-the-run gang of outlaws, there's something remarkably special about the worlds this studio creates.

With Grand Theft Auto VI approaching in just over two weeks, it's worth looking back at how that journey unfolded. From the studio's transformation and the franchises that shaped its identity to the enormous expectations around its next release, Rockstar's legacy is about much more than the games it has sold. It's about how one developer helped redefine what players expect from open-world experiences.

We’re taking this back to the humble beginnings of Rockstar Games. See, before it became one of the most popular names in the gaming landscape, its story actually began with a much smaller development team in Dundee, Scotland. Founded in 1988 by David Jones and a group of fellow developers, DMA Design started as a relatively small studio with ambitions to make its mark in an industry still finding its footing.

Its early releases, including Menace and Blood Money, showed its interest in arcade-inspired action games, but the arrival of a quirky little game called Lemmings in 1991 truly put the developer on the map. This relatively simple puzzle game (unexpectedly) became an enormous success, selling an estimated 20 million copies across its various platforms.

However, a very different kind of project would ultimately change the studio's future, since in 1997, DMA Design would then release the original Grand Theft Auto, trading its familiar arcade experiences for a top-down crime sandbox that allowed you to steal vehicles, complete odd-job missions, evade the police, and wreak havoc across fictional cities.

As the OG Grand Theft Auto continued to gain momentum despite being an experimental first entry, DMA Design underwent a series of ownership changes before becoming part of Take-Two Interactive and the wider Rockstar Games family around the turn of the millennium.

Eventually, the studio relocated from Dundee to Edinburgh, and in 2002, it officially became Rockstar North. This transformation, or turnaround, whichever one you prefer, would soon carry forward the creative foundations established years earlier. And little did you or I know just how far that journey would take them; this small Scottish team was now at the heart of a studio that would go on to produce some of the most influential open-world experiences in gaming history.

Former Rockstar technical director Obbe Vermeij recalls how GTA 3’s small team made communication easier and gave developers room to experiment.

Funnily enough, I had the chance to revisit GTA 3 this past month as part of my replay of all the mainline entries before VI’s arrival. Forgive me if it was the Definitive Edition; it was dirt-cheap on sale, and I’d already played the OG version on my PS2 as a kid, so I thought, why not try things differently, especially after this much time has passed since this trilogy’s controversial release?

Now, contrary to what the header suggests, although open-world games existed long before Grand Theft Auto III arrived, few developers had managed to bring together the same level of freedom, exploration, and interactive storytelling that Rockstar would eventually become known for. In fact, this is also why I’d like to give a shout-out to my co-worker and friend, Maddie, for discussing how 1999's Urban Chaos, developed by Mucky Foot Productions, was already experimenting with a 3D urban environment, free-roaming exploration, and mission-based gameplay two years before GTA 3 hit the PS2.

While it wasn't the expansive sandbox Rockstar would then create in later titles, it showed the potential of this simple yet experimental idea: letting players explore and interact with a full 3D city. But because it went beyond the formulaic approach of the prior two GTAs, you could absolutely make a case that this game was a generational release for its time.

Instead of simply following a predetermined series of missions, players could steal vehicles, explore different neighborhoods, interact with pedestrians, engage in shootouts, and stumble upon all sorts of unexpected chaos along the way. Driving, shooting, and exploring were no longer separate gameplay modes, but seamlessly interconnected parts of a much larger experience.

Oh, and it didn’t stop there, obviously. The game's success would go on to influence countless developers, establishing a formula that would shape much of the open-world genre for years to come, since Rockstar wasn't simply offering players a large map to explore; it was creating an environment filled with activities, distractions, and opportunities for experimentation.

Playing San Andreas was one of my most endearing experiences, with countless playthroughs/save files.

The studio continued refining that approach with Grand Theft Auto: Vice City in 2002 and then Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas in 2004. The former introduced a distinctive 1980s atmosphere reminiscent of Miami Vice’s stylized tone and an unforgettable soundtrack, while the latter expanded the formula considerably with multiple cities, character customization, and RPG-inspired mechanics.

So by the time San Andreas arrived, Rockstar had shown how much freedom and variety could fit into a single open-world experience. It is genuinely insane that these guys released three back-to-back bangers; it's an honest travesty that they outsourced the modern re-release of them to an external developer under their umbrella.

GTA 3 often ran at just 7 or 8 FPS during development, according to former Rockstar technical director Obbe Vermeij.

While Grand Theft Auto remained Rockstar's biggest commercial success, the company was never particularly interested in limiting itself to a single franchise; these guys were seriously trailblazing their way to the top. That’s because throughout the 2000s, its growing network of development studios experimented with different genres, storytelling approaches, and settings, resulting in some of its most memorable cult favorites.

Bully took the familiar open-world formula and turned it into a crude yet charming coming-of-age adventure. Meanwhile, Manhunt explored a much darker side of the company's creativity through its disturbing atmosphere (enough to give me the frights as a kid) and brutal stealth-based gameplay, and then Midnight Club brought open-city exploration into the street racing scene of the 2000s that other series like NFS also capitalized on with Fast and Furious’ popularity.

And don’t worry, like most of you, possibly longtime fans reading this, I still hold an undying grudge against Rockstar for never revisiting these games again, especially the high possibilities for a sequel to Bully, which I’m never burying the hatchet over because the Scholarship Edition is one of my most played and adored games on the Xbox 360. The bottom line is that these projects showed Rockstar's ambitions extended well beyond crime-driven satire sandboxes, allowing its various studios to establish their own identities across genres.

Rockstar Games has spent decades building some of the most recognisable worlds in video game history.

Of course, Grand Theft Auto wasn't going anywhere. And how ironic that I rolled credits on this just a week ago. With GTA IV in 2008, Rockstar took a noticeably different approach to its established formula for a grittier, more grounded portrayal of Liberty City akin to New York City.

It introduced a string of themes like revenge, organized crime overlords butting heads for power, and the often uncomfortable realities of chasing the American Dream. Plus, things like the ragdoll physics and weight-based driving model were the icing on the cake for an otherwise brilliant crime drama, one that I personally think is the best in the series in terms of writing. However, as much as I hate to admit it, Rockstar wasn't finished pushing those boundaries.

An interview with Rockstar reveals details about GTA 6's morality system.

Grand Theft Auto V arrived in 2013, taking you back to Los Santos and introducing three playable protagonists: Michael, Franklin, and Trevor. Its intertwining storytelling, enormous variety of activities, and remarkable sense of freedom made it a defining open-world release of its generation. Today, it is insane to think about how many records this game has broken: it's one of the best-selling video games of all time, second only to Minecraft, and has generated billions of dollars since its original launch.

Beyond the story mode, GTA Online (unfortunately) gradually grew into a massive multiplayer platform of its own, keeping players invested through years of updates, new missions, vehicles, heists, and activities. And I won’t lie: as someone who spent an unhealthy number of hours on it, this game was partly why I found two of my bestest friends. Also, this mode's longevity and the revenue it generated through microtransactions were low-key part of why GTA V became a cultural phenomenon that kept thriving across multiple console generations.

The wizards at Rockstar didn’t stop there, because the leap that came forward after would soon set the benchmark for people to compare most open-world releases to, even if most of those comparisons became insufferable to come across in social media posts and/or videos.

And that considerable leap came when Rockstar dropped the technical bombshell that was Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018. You see, I could’ve put the original entry in the section above with the other projects these guys did, but it only felt right to include it here, since both these two Wild West open-world titles became games that almost felt like companion pieces to the GTA franchise. That was evident not only in the mission design, but also in newer additions like the Honor system, a fully realized wildlife ecosystem, and other gameplay elements that made it feel like a sister game to GTA.

Following the success of the 2010 entry, the sequel offered a story centered around Arthur Morgan and the gradual decline of the Van der Linde gang, one that slowly connected to the events of RDR1. Its greatest achievement, however, was arguably the extraordinary level of detail packed into its bygone world. From real wildlife behavior and daily NPC routines to dynamic world events that shifted depending on the protagonist or time passed, almost every aspect of its world contributed to an incredible sense of immersion.

Although years later, you’ll now find some recent verbal engagements about people arguing about its flawed mission design, and as much as I think it's a bit overrated (please put the pitchforks down), I will wholeheartedly agree on the fact that this was THE game that made Rockstar the rightful heir to the throne for creating one of the most immersive and compelling open-world games of all time. Most importantly, it also rewarded those willing to slow down and simply enjoy their surroundings, and I think that’s the best compliment to give RDR2 given the current attention span of most mainstream audiences.

After decades of refining its approach to open-world design, Rockstar Games now stands on the doorstep of what could be its most ambitious project yet, as GTA VI represents more than just another long-awaited sequel, especially considering how much the studio has accomplished since we first stepped foot into Los Santos by repo’ing cars with Franklin and Lamar or just cruising around Ocean Beach as Tommy.

I won’t bore your ear with a bunch of what-if bumbo jumbo, but all I want to sign off with is that, given everything Rockstar has showcased so far, there's plenty of reason to be excited about the possibilities they could improve upon here, particularly when considering the technical artistry demonstrated in RDR2.

We’ve already seen an extent of the full gameplay in action with the Extended Look, as well as tons of deeper details shared online across media outlets that make this entry a proper sim-like experience, which I honestly don’t mind since I genuinely wanted Rockstar to bring back the RPG stuff they introduced back in San Andreas. Heck, even if it’s not confirmed, throw in vehicle schools again to give Lucia and Jason even more stats to manage.

For me, one of the biggest challenges GTA VI faces is delivering a story that can stand alongside GTA IV because Niko Bellic's journey for me remains one of the franchise's most memorable narratives precisely because it went beyond the usual criminal escapade trope. Most of all, it made its protagonist feel like more than another criminal navigating a fictional city, and I'd love to see Jason and Lucia achieve that in their own way.

Their relationship already gives Rockstar an interesting foundation to explore, but what matters most is whether the studio can make players genuinely care about the people behind all the chaos. Give me another round of NPC social links calling either protagonist just for a round of bowling or, y’know, give me reasons to interact with them again via their special abilities/benefits.

Now, with Leonida and the newly imagined Vice City waiting just around the corner, it feels like we're about to experience the next chapter in a legacy that has shaped how an entire generation experiences video games.

While I generally have mixed feelings about the overly eccentric fanbase, I’ll put that aside for now since I’m also proudly blasting Flower in Hurricane and Inner Light on repeat these days to itch my hype fever for the game’s release on November 19th. Whether Rockstar can deliver another landmark open-world experience remains to be seen, but hey, to anyone who made it here to see it happen, I hope we eat good with whatever they’ve cooked up over the past 13 years.

#4274. PlayStation Provides A Brief Update On PS6 Development Progress

Sony published its latest financial results today, which include an update on the PS5’s lifetime sales. There’s also a note on the development of the PS6, and it’s really starting to sound like it might be full steam ahead on a 2028 launch for PlayStation’s next-gen console.

“Looking ahead to the next fiscal year, we aim to continue to enhance user engagement and further strengthen monetization through the release of strong titles and the expansion of our service,” Sony CFO Lin Tao said during today’s financial results (thanks, VGC), adding, “We also intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform .”

“From next fiscal year onward, there will be investment in the new platform. For future growth, we have to attach great importance to a new platform and make the necessary investments for that,” Tao continued, clarifying that an announcement on the specifics will be made at an appropriate time in the future.

A renewed focus on PS6 development during the next fiscal year, which will begin in April 2027, certainly sounds like the plan is for PlayStation to have its next console ready for release at some point in 2028. Likely towards the end of the year, similar to the PS5 launch in November 2025.

Particularly when, during the same financial call, Tao also noted that even though PS5 sales are still on the rise - PlayStation’s latest console has now sold 97.9 million units - the rate at which they are being sold is “gradually declining as expected”. Not only because the console is six years old, but because memory shortages and rising RAM costs mean a new PS5 is now considerably more expensive than it was in 2020.

Speaking of memory and its rising costs, one of the more positive reveals made during the financial call was confirmation that PlayStation has secured enough of it to see it through the next fiscal year. That presumably means the one starting in April, and suggests that, if development on the PS6 really starts to hit its stride, then there’s enough RAM to go around for further PS5 production, and for the early stages of the PS6.

That hopefully means, for now at least, console price rises won’t affect PlayStation again for the foreseeable future. The company is already struggling to get new stock out there due to memory shortages, which is why it sent out a notification this week urging those not using their PS5 to trade them in.

It really needs PS5s on store shelves, even if they’re refurbished ones, with new customers hunting them out ready for GTA 6.

It would seem that, despite rising RAM prices, global shortages, and most people seemingly being fine to sit with their PS5s for a lot longer than usual due to how much its replacement will potentially cost, we’re getting a PS6 within the next two years whether we like it or not. It also seems likely that the console will cost upwards of $1,000, with the suggestion that Xbox’s Project Helix could cost anything between $1,200 and $1,800.

Sony's refusal to change course has been further highlighted as new PS5 boxes warn about 2028 changes.

#4272. Grammy Award-Winning Composer Austin Wintory Shares His Early Musical Drafts Intended For Mass Effect 5

Last week, EA shut down Mass Effect and Dragon Age developer BioWare, which resulted in the cancellation of the fifth Mass Effect game that was announced in 2020. As the fallout from this closure settles, famed video game composer Austin Wintory has shared that he'd been working on a potential soundtrack for the now-canceled game and has publicly released early versions of this score.

In a Bluesky thread, Wintory, who has composed soundtracks for games such as Journey, Sword of the Sea (for which he won a Grammy), Assassin’s Creed: Syndicate, and The Banner Saga trilogy, writes, “Mass Effect was my ultimate white whale, my all-time dream project. For the last couple years I'd been in discussion w/ BioWare & EA to take on the project & as part of that I wrote close to 20 minutes of music to explore where the franchise can go next, may as well share it!"

Wintory uploaded a 20-minute video consisting of eight tracks to his YouTube channel. The video begins with a message further elaborating on the partnership between BioWare, EA, and him. “For the past several years, I’d been in dialogue with people both at BioWare and EA to potentially jump into Mass Effect 5. As part of these conversations, I decided to surprise the team by writing/recording a gigantic love letter to the franchise, with my idea of where it can go next.”

Wintory adds that he composed the music in 2025 and that he “knew nothing” about what Mass Effect 5's story entailed when he did. As such, he describes the music as “narratively speculative.” He adds that this conceptual soundtrack was a direct homage to Jack Wall and Sam Hulick’s soundtrack on the first Mass Effect “while leaning even harder on true analog synths, and a more complex integration of the orchestra (almost akin to the hybrid nature of The Matrix),” he writes. Each music track features a message by Wintory explaining his inspiration for its production.

“Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss," Wintory writes in the video's description. "It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever. Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much.”

Wintory's music is the latest piece of potential Mass Effect 5 content to emerge since BioWare’s closure. A day after the shutdown announcement, an unreleased but reportedly legitimate cinematic trailer for the canceled Mass Effect leaked online.

#4271. App Army Assemble: Crushed In Time - "Is this comedic point-and-click adventure a must-play?"

Crushed In Time is yet another point-and-click adventure from the folks behind There Is No Game: Wrong Dimension. Given that our App Army is familiar with the team's previous work, we decided to ask them if Draw Me A Pixel's latest effort is worth playing.

Crushed In Time is a beautifully animated cartoon-style adventure following the iconic duo of Sherlock Holmes and Dr John Watson. While the game falls into the traditional point-and-click genre, you’ll actually be using a rather fun “catch and stretch” mechanic that works really well on your touchscreen device. The presentation is all top-notch, everything looks simply gorgeous, and the excellent dialogue is superbly voice-acted, keeping you glued to the screen throughout.

The puzzles here can get challenging at times; I often found myself resorting to some trial and error. Luckily, there’s a really nice hint system that’s available to alleviate any difficulties you may run into, which you can use at your discretion. I loved my time spent with Crushed In Time - two thumbs up!

This is a fun point-and-click adventure. The cartoon graphics are appealing. The stretch and release system is unique and adds to the atmosphere; the occasional fourth-wall breaking and British humour make it fun. Fun enough to make up for the initial frustration.

I needed the hint system a lot early on, but less as I started to get the groove of the game. And yeah, I’m pretty much always up for some time travel hills. In an App Store full of point-and-click games (that I’m honestly not a huge fan of, mostly because I’m not always good at them?) This one rises above the pack thanks to its relentless fun and humour. Definitely worth trying for free.

I was expecting a point-and-click adventure, and then I noticed the developers are the same ones responsible for the There Is No Game game. And that's how we get a very ingenious slingshot-and-click game instead of a classic point-and-click. So, the fourth wall breaks in this Sherlock Holmes reimagination adventure with some time travel added to the mix, where we need to stretch everything and every object on screen to make things happen or move. Our heroes feel that something paranormal is happening around them (shhh, don't tell them—it's our hand doing the paranormal stuff, the hand of God). With a lot of humour everywhere, you can see the characters complaining for something to happen.

Then, we make it happen by stretching something or activating an object by means of rotation, and they will take credit for whatever happened. The puzzles are fun to solve, and there's a hint system in place if you don't like to rely on trial and error so much. A lot of physics is involved in how we manipulate objects and people to make things happen. I must say I'm having a lot of fun with this game. The mechanics and controls are very innovative; the voice acting and humour are superb, as are the graphics, animations, and the Indiana Jones-like soundtrack. There aren't a lot of games like this one, that's for sure. If you're into point-and-click games, or just games completely outside the box, this one is surely for you.

Crushed in Time is a good-looking point-and-click adventure. A game within a game, as a mysterious letter sends Holmes and Watson on a journey. The novelty here is that you manipulate the characters and objects by stretching and releasing areas of the screen. The cartoon graphics and voice acting are good, and there is an excellent hint system. The stretching mechanic can be frustrating at times; it took me a while just to wake up Holmes at the start. Recommended if you like this type of game.

Crushed in Time is overall brilliant and unique in terms of controls, as things work with elastic controls (instead of tap or button control, we have to grab, pull, and release). I love the comedic theme, superb writing and voiceovers. The puzzles work like magic, especially because of those unique controls. Cartoon graphics work like charm, and also a shout-out for giving amazing animation work when we interact with the world in the game.

Crushed in Time is a fourth-wall-breaking British humour puzzle where the linear adventure game approach with all of its typical crazy inventory combinations is replaced by physics-based gameplay and some tricky timing combos too. The conceit is that the game developers have lost control of their code, so the in-game characters must traverse the program and save the day by setting the environment to rights.

Does it work? Yes... and no. The generous use of “point-and-click game logic” often means you’ll rely on a great deal of trial and error (or the hint system) to find the exact solution dreamed up by a specific developer rather than something you think should work. While that’s typical of p&c games in general, it’s doubled down on here due to the stretch-and-release game mechanic, which works better on a touch screen than on a computer.

Beautiful graphics, inventive approach to puzzle solving (which fails as often as it succeeds), silly humour, good music and voice work all add up to something worth trying. Fortunately, there’s a lengthy demo if you want to try before buying. The full game runs about 6 hours of playtime. Recommended if you can stand frustration. Best in short bursts.

I haven’t played a point-and-click style game in a long time and my first go with one in many years being this was quite difficult! First off, it looks great, and it not being fullscreen surprisingly didn’t bother me at all because I was so engrossed in the gameplay and story, which is all voice-acted.

Now I say it was quite difficult; maybe that’s just because I’m not used to point-and-clicks anymore? Or because they change things up by having it be a stretching mechanic that helps puzzles in clever ways.

If you like point-and-click style games and their puzzles and have the patience to figure them out or use the very handy hint system, which I try not to use as I consider it cheating, but sometimes you just get stumped! But if that part is fun for you rather than stressful, then this is a great game, and I’m sure you wouldn’t be let down picking it up at all, especially as I said before, with the fully voice-acted story to keep you interested and wanting more. #4270. Gunboat God sets November launch date for its crocodile-powered shoot 'em up

Getting home involves shooting just about everything in sight

Your mechanic in Gunboat God is a crocodile called Yeti. I’ve read that back a few times now and it still doesn’t make any more sense, but he’s apparently the best in the trade and a genuinely good guy, so I’ll stop asking questions. He’s heading to iOS and Android with the rest of this side-scrolling shoot ’em up, and to Switch as well.

You’re stuck somewhere you don’t recognise, trying to get back to a Citadel in the sky, and the best thing you’ve got is a boat with an alarming amount of firepower bolted to it. Getting home means going through more than twenty mission types. Collision Course and Outlast explain themselves, while one is just called Boil.

There are eight guns to master, cannons and lasers among them, alongside something called the Vaporiser that I’m choosing to believe isn’t a kettle. Each gets its own upgrades, and there are more than ten abilities and augments for the boat on top.

It transforms mid-level too, diving below the surface or lifting off above it, which helps when there are mines underneath and acid rain overhead. Seventy enemy types and a run of multi-phase bosses stand between you and home, spread over 180 levels.

On mobile, Gunboat God is going the try-before-you-buy route. The first biome is free with no adverts, and you pay to unlock the rest. Premium shoot ’em ups are a hard sell on phones and a free slice should answer most questions directly.

The catch is how far the slice goes. If the first biome ends on one of those multi-phase bosses, you’ll know whether the touch controls keep up once the screen fills with bullets, and that’s the test this genre lives or dies on.

Gunboat God launches on November 17th for iOS and Android.

Our list of the best shooters on iOS has a lot of guns and, to my knowledge, no reptiles on staff.

#4269. Free-To-Play MOBA Pokémon Unite Is Shutting Down In March

The free-to-play MOBA Pokémon Unite will shut down in March, over five years after its 2021 launch. Although a gradual suspension of services begins today, fans will enjoy one last hurrah thanks to a big in-game event running for the remainder of the game’s lifecycle.

Launched in July 2021 for Switch before migrating to iOS and Android later that year, Pokémon Unite was billed as a friendlier take on the MOBA genre popularized by Dota 2 and League of Legends, thanks to its short matches (10 minutes) and simplified mechanics. Despite its initial popularity, the game is winding down and will go offline for good on March 23, 2027.

An End of Service notice on the game’s website reads,

“We offer our sincerest gratitude to the many Trainers who have played since service started for the Nintendo Switch version on July 21, 2021. We would like to express our thanks to everyone by holding a special event until service ends. The Pokémon Unite Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo competitive tournament (an event for Pokémon Unite only) will also be held as previously announced. We hope you continue to enjoy Pokémon Unite until the final day of service. After service ends, the 'Pokémon Unite Game Content Guidelines for Online Platforms' will no longer be published or maintained, and we will no longer provide support regarding use of Pokémon Unite videos and images.”

As of today, in-game sales of Aeos gems and Unite Club memberships/renewals have been suspended. Existing Unite Club members will continue to use their benefits until the end of the membership period.

On November 12, an update will kick off the aforementioned final special event, where players can obtain items such as all Unite licenses and Holoware that have appeared in the game up to that point. A library feature will also be added, letting players view certain records and in-game content even after the game shuts down on March 23. Those who don’t download the library feature before the shutdown date will not be able to get it afterward.

Qualifiers for the Aeos Crown 2027 Tokyo Competitive tournament will take place as planned on December 5. After the game shuts down on March 23, players won't be able to log in to Pokémon Unite or play any battles. Only the library feature will remain accessible.

We enjoyed Pokémon Unite when it launched, with executive video editor Alex Van Aken scoring it an 8 out of 10 in his review, writing, “The game eats away the hours of my day as I reassuringly say to myself, 'Just one more match.' Battles play out with the spectacle that the Pokémon series is known for, and with so many abilities to choose from, no match feels the same as the last. The game’s simple mechanics and recognizable characters make for an approachable MOBA experience, and with a potential catalog of nearly 900 Pokémon to pick from, my hopes are high for the future of Pokémon Unite.”

#4268. Infinity Nikki ushers in the Year of the Horse with... a deer-themed Version 2.2

Chromatic Beings Everbright, the latest major Infinity Nikki update, has arrived, bringing Chinese New Year celebrations vibe to the game.

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, open-world dress-up RPG, has delivered yet another big content drop in the form of Chromatic Beings Everbright. The latest update brings the game up to version 2.2, and introduces a new narrative chapter, and gameplay taking place around a festival narrative.

If you couldn’t guess already, the new theme is Bloom Festival, inspired by Chinese New Year celebrations.

The big new story chapter takes place in the Infinity Nikki’s Wanxiang Realm. This deceptively serene and blissful region hides a dark secret, however. Chromafaces, the mythical inhabitants of the realm, have to embody fixed identities that dictate how they live and work.

These are doled out through Character Tokens, which are used to assign roles to each individual. The story follows Nikki as she uncovers the script that runs the realm and the facade it props up. Nikki will help free Chromafaces and dispel the illusion.

The Wanxiang Realm is split into three areas. Cai Ye is your typical lantern-lit district, where festivals and fireworks happen. Kongming Gorge is almost the opposite of that; a quiet and cold place. Finally, Jiuhua Pavilion literally floats above the region, and it's home to neverending music and dance.

The other big addition in 2.2 are the two new 5-Star Resonance Outfits with some interesting gameplay implications. Where Wanxiang Weaves Life is inspired by wuxia aesthetics, and true to its inspirations, it lets Nikki shapeshift into different Spirit Personas - and automatically collect resources in her vicinity.

Chroma's Mortal Heart, on the other hand, allows Nikki to fly around the Wanxiang Realm, drawing on the power of the Celestial Deer. This outfit also uses Celestial Deer Vision to automatically ping and mark treasure chests around her.

You can also look forward to Nefarious Shadows, a new Ability Outfit, which lets Nikki see through disguises, and reveals hidden paths in the world.

As with every major update, of course, there are themed activities and limited-time events throughout. Hotpot House is a cooking minigame where you attempt to run the eponymous restaurant, whereas Flavor Frenzy is series of platforming challenges that tasks you with gathering ingredients. Fortune Mahjong is a little more straightforward, with support for solo and multiplayer play.
