#4265. French Union Accuses Microsoft of Deadlocking Marvel’s Blade

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Many studios have been in rough patches recently, either due to internal struggles amid the modern challenges of development or due to layoffs or closures mandated by larger owners. It's easy to write off every issue in the modern industry as someone else’s fault, but that’s not realistic; every part of the industry is struggling, inside and out.

The upcoming God of War spin-off has been delayed to May 20th, dodging the busy February release window.

Arkane Lyon is one studio that's been in hot water for a long while, struggling to find a buyer before Microsoft closes its doors. Following hopeful news as more buyers step up, a French union with ties to Arkane staff has accused Microsoft of attempting to sabotage the development of the studio’s current project, Blade, by barring hires for over a year.

The development of Marvel’s Blade has been absolutely hectic, between internal shifts in the game’s vision and an early announcement that put heat on Arkane far before they were ready. Now, STJV, the French union representing certain members of Arkane Lyon’s staff, has made a major accusation, claiming the game is coming along fine, despite Microsoft’s interference.

According to STJV in a direct quotation, “Today, as work on Blade is going fine, and the level of quality of the game to be expected is on [par] with what Arkane has accustomed its players, workers have to face the harsh reality: our studio might get closed because, and only because, Microsoft decided to, even if that means sabotaging the game it funded.”

This all still has yet to be confirmed, as no direct response from Microsoft has been released, despite the accusations levied by STJV. Alongside the biting remarks, the union has dropped a series of demands, including a say in who buys Arkane, and a larger payout for the staff if no buyer steps forward.

It's easy to write off every issue in the modern industry as someone else’s fault, but that’s not realistic, every part of the industry is struggling, inside and out.

Despite all of this swinging out, Arkane is still eager to release Blade, staying optimistic that the title will release in the following years if Arkane is allowed to keep their doors open. STJV keeps the argument practical, framing the studio’s progress as a financial incentive for both parties. “Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game,” says STJV.

Arkane’s aim to finish the game despite their wild situation is comforting to see, and gives me real hope at the quality of their Blade title, as long as it manages to release. The whispers of big studios like Ubisoft’s interest make it clear more than just Arkane want to see the title released, and as the months continue to tick by with the company still open, those whispers just get louder.

Arkane is a studio that would feel like a serious loss for the larger gaming industry if they closed their doors, even after stumbles like Redfall. Dropping into the mainstream scene with hits like Dishonored and Prey, Arkane Lyon is infamous for worlds that feel so lived-in, even after devastation has raked across them.

They truly do feel like the perfect team to work on Blade, as their mastery of immersive sims and wild powers leaves massive room for the exact type of action Blade is perfect for. It really does feel like every production surrounding Blade is hexed, if the canceled films and Arkane’s own pains are anything to look at.

I’m very eager to hear a response from Microsoft, as STJV has levied some major accusations that could really disrupt how third parties and internal studios interact with them. At present, we only have STJV’s word to go off of, so take these accusations with a grain of salt until more comes out.

#4262. Phantom Blade Zero Review – Wuxia Wonder Abounds

Rooted in Wuxian storytelling and scale, built on an impressively detailed combat system, and wrapped in a bloody Chinese martial underground that’s a genuine joy to play in, Phantom Blade Zero is a feat. It joins an echelon of action pedigree that includes Sekiro, Devil May Cry, Bayonetta, and just about any other action game you hold in high regard. It hails from developer S-Game, which has dabbled in mobile and smaller-scale games, and I’m shocked by what it’s pulled off with its triple-A action inauguration. But make no mistake: though Phantom Blade Zero is this team’s first crack at a game like this, it is an incredibly confident, strong debut.

Protagonist Soul is a stoic martial arts master betrayed by the Order he’s sworn his life to; he dies and returns to life with only 66 days to live. That’s enough time to settle his debts, repay his betrayers, and end a villainous conspiracy to seize full power of the Wulin realm. This narrative is Phantom Blade Zero's weakest link, but its premise adds enough mystery and tension to keep this Wuxian journey exciting through to its final, realm-shattering moments. Narrative bombshells drop not just through the game’s general fantasy-realism art direction, but also through anime scenes, opera puppet shows, animated brushstroke sequences, and more, highlighting Chinese culture and its integral place in Phantom Blade Zero.

The game features a staggering number of unique enemy types, and though the final hours get a bit repetitive, it’s admirable how long S-Game maintains such a high level of combat-oriented ecstasy. Soul’s access to weapons drives that exhilaration. Every weapon is wholly unique. Because the combat is combo-based, picking up a new weapon feels like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. Each has its own moveset and abilities, with later-game weapons featuring combo lists that look more at home in a Street Fighter menu. Add in the special, tide-turning weapons known as Phantom Edges, with limited charge-based uses, and there’s no shortage of permutations to delightfully experiment with.

Drawing on Chinese cinema, Phantom Blade Zero's setpiece bosses boast a sense of awe and scale only the genre's best typically offer. With virtually no repeat bosses, save for a few in separate trials, it’s impressive how many powerful figures I flayed, and how many delivered a unique fight. I also appreciate the checkpoints between boss phases, as they remove the frustrating repetition of replaying phase one again and again just to take another stab at the second phase I’m struggling with.

You’d be forgiven for assuming Phantom Blade Zero is a Soulslike, given its challenging bosses, interconnected world, and Phantom Bell checkpoints, this game’s equivalent of bonfires. It definitively isn’t, though. The challenge is much more surmountable; the game isn’t interested in making you die over and over, there are difficulty options, and you can equip accessories to make parries and dodges easier. World progression is materially different, too, as enemies don’t respawn after you kill them. It’s an interesting, perhaps blasphemous, choice for the genre, but it's surprisingly effective, adding a sense of worldbuilding and tangible progression I didn’t know I wanted from my action games. Soul is on a mission to remove evil, and mechanically, I’m doing just that. Enemies don’t respawn incoherently just because I heal and save.

Environmental features weave in and out of each other, and the architectural design and layout of these regions lead to many subsequent “aha” moments. S-Game infuses search-action elements into this exploration through the aforementioned Phantom Edges, some of which double as tools to unlock surprising new areas in both new and previously visited biomes. As a result, backtracking and exploration remain fresh. A lot of it is optional, as are some of Phantom Blade Zero's most rewarding elements, including its demanding “perfect” ending. Sadly, this renders other endings unsatisfying, with clear chunks intentionally missing.

Despite forays into the Uncanny Valley, Phantom Blade Zero is visually striking, and the action is brilliantly animated. It’s all set to genre-breaking music, too, with original metalcore songs, operatic choirs, 808s, and traditional Chinese instrumentation, creating a score as illustrious as the action it enhances.

Phantom Blade Zero is an astounding action achievement, almost unbelievably so for a game that is essentially a studio’s genre debut. It is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, one that recognizes the genre’s strengths and weaknesses and addresses both with fantastical Wuxian style. Though the action genre is always jam-packed with new releases, few are as special as Phantom Blade Zero.

Angels of Delusion is also the group that the two new Agents being introduced in this update belong to. Members of the same group are capable of performing coordinated attacks. The new arrivals are Sunna and Aria.

Yet another login event - Gilded Surprise, Wonderful Boo-ns - will be available February 14-23, offering daily draws from a pool of 4 billion Polychrome.

#4259. Starsand Island is a life and farming sim that isn't gacha, and it's out next week

Starsand Island officially has an Early Access release date, and it sounds like it won't stay there for years.

Though it may seem like we just had a big life sim release in Heartopia, 2026 actually has more than one highly-anticipated release in that particular subgenre of cozy game. The next big one on the horizon is Starsand Island, the life and farming sim from Seed Sparkle Lab.

The game has been gaining momentum since the launch of a demo in October last year, but the developer never quite managed to commit to a date for its debut title. Until now.

Seed Sparkle Lab announced today that Starsand Island will enter Early Access on February 11, which is only a bit over one week from now. This goes for Steam and the Xbox Preview Program version.

The developer said to expect a fairly short Early Access run, as the full launch is expected in the summer of this year. When the full release arrives, the game will also make the jump to PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series, as well as Switch 2.

The full release is also expected to bring Steam Deck support and introduce the multiplayer mode, which will not be available during Early Access

Starsand Island has something of a unique look compared to other games in the subgenre. The storybook, anime-inspired aesthetics are popular in the realm of gacha games, of course. However, seeing as this particular game isn’t gacha, being a premium product means it’s going to offer something free-to-play games aren’t designed to.

Speaking of which, the game will be available in two editions: Standard and Deluxe, with the latter including Romanticism-inspired outfits, furniture, and other customisation items. If you buy either during launch, you’ll also get a Chinese New Year bonus with even more outfits and furniture.

On top of the usual systems of farming, mining, and making friends with adorable characters (and animals), the game also has combat that pits you against ancient guardians. You can, of course, also build a home in it, and decorate it to your heart's content.

Seed Sparkle Lab says you can expect about 100 hours of content in the Early Access launch build, and more features will arrive over the course of the next six or so months, including a crossover event with My Time At Portia.

#4256. Nioh 3 launches, immediately becomes the most played Nioh ever on Steam

Just a few hours after launch, Nioh 3 is already the biggest release in series history on Steam.

It sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. #4255. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4253. Nintendo Indie World Showcase Recap: Everything We Saw

The year is nearing its conclusion, and the last big AAA titles are rolling out one-by-one. But today, it was all about the independent titles on Nintendo's latest Indie World Showcase, highlighting new games from smaller indie teams coming to the Switch and Switch 2.

Here's everything we saw at the October 2026 Nintendo Indie World Showcase.

Today's Indie World Showcase started with a big headliner, as the long-awaited witch-life simulator Witchbrook got a release date. Chucklefish and Robtality's cozy magical world goes live on January 28, 2027.

Fans of 3D platformers should probably keep an eye on Winds of Viridia, which looks like a colorful game with a lot of interesting movement and exploration. Shark Jump's fantastical platformer is arriving next year, but if the wait's too long, a free demo is coming today on the eShop.

From one of the co-creators of Celeste, City of None has a gorgeous pixelated art style and colors that immediately remind me of Game Boy Color classics. It's a 2D platformer where you leap around, fight enemies, and explore the strange city around you. The jumping and fighting look solid, and I really like the mysterious atmosphere and art direction. City of None's set for sometime in 2027.

The sword-surfing adventure from the makers of Abzu and Journey is coming to Nintendo Switch 2 on October 29, 2026 - tomorrow! It's a gorgeous adventure that earned a Must-Play badge from us, so it's worth your time if you like the kinds of gorgeous, beautiful adventures Giant Squid (developer of Abzu) is known for.

Take an overhead camera angle, brawler gameplay, and some John Wick sensibilities, and you've got Tenjutsu, a stylish roguelike where you use your martial arts prowess to tear apart crime syndicates. I really enjoy the look and vibe of this one, and it's from one of the designers of Dead Cells, too. Tenjutsu might be one to keep an eye on when it arrives on Switch 2 in 2027.

RPG fans have been eating well, and it looks like the feast could continue next year with Threads of Time. The time-traveling RPG is coming to both Switch and Switch 2 next summer, and it's looking absolutely gorgeous.

Ah, raccoons. Nature's most adorable little scamps. If you and your friends have ever wanted to live out the dream of being a rambunctious band of raccoons wreaking havoc on the town, Dumpster Gang sets out to give you just that fantasy in March 2027.

I've already enjoyed quite a bit of Super Battle Golf on PC, so I'll tell you now: if you enjoy golf games and want some Mario Party annoy-your-friends antics wound around them, Super Battle Golf should be on your radar for its March 25, 2027 launch on Switch 2.

Another port of a PC multiplayer mainstay, the co-op physics-driven horror-looter R.E.P.O. is coming to Switch 2 in 2027. This is one for the crowd that likes to be scared one moment and laughing hysterically the next.

Rounding out the co-op section, Haunted Paws has you and a pal playing as a pair of pups searching for their person in a haunted mansion. The side-scrolling 3D look makes it seem like a less-scary Little Nightmares, and the concept is pretty fun. Look for this one on Switch and Switch 2 in May 2027, or try out the free demo later today.

#4249. Sonic Pico Park Review: A Great Party Favor

Sonic the Hedgehog becomes friends with the cute little cats of Pico Park, inviting all of us into a co-op puzzle-platformer that's sure to make you laugh one way or another.

This year marks the big 3-5 for Sega’s patented Mario killer, Sonic the Hedgehog. It’s been an eventful time for all kinds of fans. Of course, it’s hard to celebrate this momentous occasion with the all but ignored elephant in the room that is the mainline game Sonic Team has all but officially unveiled that’s still in development. But we aren’t going without a game for the anniversary, at least!

Enter Sonic Pico Park. Like the title implies, it’s a return to the chaotic co-op world of Pico Park with a new hedgehog-shaped coat of paint. Ever since it was announced in time for the blue blur’s birthday, Sonic Pico Park has been teasing the mechanics and playable characters slowly leading up to the game’s November launch. It’s been a nice little treat between Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds DLC, monthly comics, and a stream of other goodies throughout the year. But there’s a question that I’m sure a lot of us want to ask.

Sonic the Hedgehog is turning 35 this year, and if you're looking for games to celebrate the occasion, there are plenty of options for you.

Is Sonic Pico Park a good game for this milestone? Is it as good and as cute as it’s been advertised? Is it more Pico than Sonic? Luckily for you, I’m here to answer these questions and more. A short answer to keep things quick: Yes, and no. And if that makes you happy, let’s get into deeper details so you know what you’re getting into before dragging your friends into playing with you.

I’ll be honest and say that it’s hard for me to not fall victim to Sonic Pico Park’s charms. I’ve always adored sprite art. Seeing some of my favorite characters of all time as these miniaturized, big-headed versions, dancing around and reflecting their personalities in these quick animations is just too good to resist. But there’s more to Sonic Pico Park than that.

Like the original Pico Park, Sonic Pico Park is a co-op game where teamwork is key to win. It can be played with at least two players, but you can navigate this game with eight people max if you really want these short and sweet levels to be complete ragers in two different senses of the word. I got to team up with two other writers to play this game. The fun of Sonic Pico Park definitely grows with the number of players involved.

The puzzling co-op of Pico Park fits like a glove with Sonic’s trademark speed. If you thought the original Pico Park may have been too slow, this game picks up the pace with ease without making anything too uncontrollable or without giving you and your friends time to think things through. There are fewer twists to the levels that gave Pico Park what fame it has here, though, likely to keep things less frustrating for younger players and their families. Saboteurs who purposefully ignore instructions for a laugh will still have their ways, though.

Plenty of Pico Park gimmicks, like buttons, numbered platforms and blocks, are scattered throughout the level with springs, loop-de-loops, and rings from Sonic. There are more Sonic mechanics to play with throughout the whole game than Pico staples, and there are plenty of surprises for the average Sonic fan to spot. It’s because of these features that Sonic Pico Park really sticks out as a Sonic game, and one that certainly rises to the 35th anniversary occasion. But like most parties, it will end and become a good memory in time.

One important factor Sonic fans should understand before jumping into Sonic Pico Park is that the games that came before it aren’t particularly long. Pico Park itself only takes about three hours, and I managed to play everything the game offered in about four and a half hours according to my playtime stats. Thankfully this balances out with Sonic Pico Park’s asking price, which I think is fair for a cute little romp with friends. Especially since all it takes is for one of those friends to choose violence and a level that would take five minutes has now taken fifteen because everyone’s too busy laughing and screaming to get back on track. You know. Typical co-op game stuff.

As a Sonic game, Sonic Pico Park is a great snack for the hungry, but won’t be enough for the ravenous.

Sonic fans will still have fun seeing the unexpected twists to what Pico Park is known for. If you remove the Sonic flavoring, you can still find a fun platformer underneath, but the personality of each of the playable Sonic characters really completes the experience. It gives it a sense of style that blends both games together to create something unique that fans will love. It might also serve as the perfect gateway for any Sonic-obsessed friends to finally pull you into this series. Play at your own risk.

Without going into too many details, Sonic Pico Park sticks the landing as an anniversary game. There are a lot of surprises to find in this game as you go along, but it comes at the price of the game’s identity at times that might rub a few players the wrong way. There’s an element to Pico Park that remains in these moments, bringing in a new challenge of figuring out how to tackle the old with the new. But that might not be enough to save these moments from feeling like jingling keys to a fan worn out on the last decade or so of nostalgic references.

Still, that’s only a more cynical look at things. Among the game’s levels and modes, I feel like there are far more interesting twists on Sonic mechanics with Pico Park-style platforming and puzzle-solving than anything else. As a Sonic game, Sonic Pico Park is a great snack for the hungry, but won’t be enough for the ravenous. But it might satiate them a little if their friends bring the laughs and some good nibbles to go with it.

Any newcomers to Sonic don’t have to worry much. Sonic Pico Park doesn’t overstay its welcome. There are a few modes to play on the side, and you can always drag more friends into the chaos and not backseat them, but otherwise, it’s hard to see groups of friends coming back to Sonic Pico Park after clearing everything the first time. And sometimes, it’s okay if a party doesn’t last forever. What’s important is the chaos and fun you have with the people you share it with that will stay with you long after those few hours are up.

Sonic Pico Park is a step up for the iconic puzzle-platformer. It adds a sense of style and quick-thinking that only Sonic could bring to Pico Park while giving an element of chaos not entirely new to Sonic, but elevated through the humor of Pico Park. The dedication and love to the Sonic series can be felt in everything it squeezes into its short run time, as well as how every single character’s personality is made far bigger than the sprites used to portray them. It might not be the game fans expected out of this year, but it’s certainly what they need and deserve. Sonic Pico Park, like the games that came before it, will bring plenty of laughs and good memories to players long after this anniversary is over.

#4248. 5 new mobile games to try this week - November 5th, 2026

Fresh mobile picks you should give a go this week

Who doesn't love new games? We certainly do - there's just something about the exhilaration of a new title you can't wait to dive into, as the loading screen pops up and you enter a brave new world.

Of course, new mobile games are a dime a dozen these days, and who has the time to scour the iPhone, iPad and/or Android stores to catch the latest title that drops? Fret not - we've gathered a quick list of 5 new mobile games you should try this week, whether that's an undiscovered indie gem or a high-profile AAA masterpiece.

That said, you can head on over to our NEW WEEKLY MOBILE GAMES hub if you're on the hunt for more curated adventures to obsess over!

I suppose there's nothing quite like the end of the month than being reminded of your adulting responsibilities, which is probably why Bills Must Be Paid picked November 1st for an official launch. As you might expect from the title, this incremental clicker will have you struggling to, well, pay the bills - but the cathartic thing about it is that you'll at least get the satisfaction of smashing piggy banks out of it.

You'll have all kinds of hammers at your disposal for said piggy bank smashing, which, of course, costs stamina. You can't let exhaustion get the better of you, though, because, as you well know, bills must be paid - and bankruptcy quite literally means game over.

Absolum's art style was what initially caught my eye here, but honestly, the fact that it's a roguelite beat 'em up is already more than enough to pique my interest. This time around, the action-packed side-scroller is bringing mobile-optimised controls to the fray, with customisable buttons you can tinker around with to keep the four varied heroes you can choose from in tip-top shape.

And with full controller support, co-op gameplay, and cross-progression on mobile and PC, I'd say Talamh's in good hands!

I've been seeing this backpack management trend a lot lately, and given I've played my fair share of them recently, I'm not at all complaining! This time, SuperPlanet's putting the world of Stonia on offer, and despite the seemingly cutesy title (and art style), it's actually a much grimmer setting than you might expect.

The continent is apparently turning into dungeons, and it's up to Dungeon Supporter Mika to save the world. You'll step into each tile not knowing what it holds, but whether it's a fatal trap you're falling into or a bloodthirsty Mimic waiting for the right moment, you'll need to use your powers of backpack organisation to survive every run. It's the backpack handler's job to give those ungrateful heroes their supplies, after all, so you're pretty much the true hero here.

If you've still got a Halloween hangover, perhaps a little bit of Jekyll and Hyde might suffice? Heir of the Dog takes the classic tale and adds a humorous twist to it, and with charming pixel art to boot! The point-and-click mystery will have you searching high and low across Victorian London for clues on a missing dog, with plenty of hilarious hijinks in between.

The main protagonist is named Cummerbund Bandersnatch, for one thing. For another, it takes inspiration from Monty Python, so you know you're in for a treat - if you're up for shelling out $14.99 a pop!

Cute cats in a mobile game is a plus as it is in my book - even more so when there's multiple copies of them! This aptly titled platformer tasks you with creating copies of yourself to solve tricky puzzles across a strange lab, where you can use your titular Copy Cats to stack up high and reach unreachable places.

You might even need to manipulate your clones just to get your main cat to the exit, because when there's a missing cat involved, you need to do everything in your power to help it find its way back home.

#4244. Wolverine Has Sold Fewer Copies In 50 Days Than Spider-Man 2 Sold In Just One

Wolverine had an uncharacteristically rocky launch for Insomniac, and it looks like its reviews and the backlash towards some of its less popular mechanics may have had an impact on sales after all. While the game has sold in the millions, it’s not as many millions as you might expect from a game with one of Marvel’s most popular heroes as the lead.

Sony published its latest financial report today, and within it are updates on how well some of its first-party games have sold. Even though the report only covers the most recent quarter, which ended on September 30, 2026, it has sales figures for Wolverine’s first 50 days, right up until November 4.

According to those figures, Wolverine has sold through 2.4 million copies. That’s a big number. A number that most studios would bite your hand off for. However, those aren’t Marvel numbers, as is demonstrated by how well Spider-Man 2 sold at launch, which you can see from the webslinger’s figures a few rows up on the same Sony document.

According to that document, Spider-Man 2 sold 2.5 million copies during its first 24 hours. That means, despite having 50 times longer to hit that target, Wolverine has still fallen short. There’s an argument to be made that it’s unfair to compare the two, but it’s also unfair to suggest there is such a disparity between how well-known the heroes are that it should take Wolverine 50 times longer to hit the same targets.

There is no world in which a Wolverine game is, or was ever expected to, sell anywhere close to as well as a Spider-Man game. Spider-Man is among the most popular and recognizable characters on the planet. You give people the chance to be him in a video game, and even if that game is bad, it will sell tens of millions of copies.

Thankfully, none of them are. All three of Insomniac’s Spidey games are critically acclaimed and well-loved by fans.

Wolverine, while also immensely popular, doesn’t have that same cache, and therefore doesn’t have the luxury of his games selling millions just because his face is on the cover. While that has still happened to an extent, word getting out that the game might not be up to Insomniac’s Spidey standard seems to have had an effect, and stunted sales to a greater degree than PlayStation would have expected.

Despite the pre-launch discourse, Wolverine is a hit with fans.

With Crossy Road Rush bringing the same colourful, blocky visuals of the original to Apple Arcade, not to mention new, fast-paced gameplay that'll challenge even endless runner veterans, I think it's well worth taking a look at if you're on Apple Arcade!

But in the meantime, if you play on Android or simply aren't privy to Apple Arcade's extensive library, don't fret. There's plenty of other options to play on our list of the best mobile games of 2026 (so far), which features choice picks from the last 11 months!

#4241. Here's The Best Graphics And Performance Mode For Phantom Blade Zero On PlayStation 5

Phantom Blade Zero is out now for everyone as a console exclusive on PlayStation 5 and on PC via Steam and the Epic Games Store as well. If you missed it, it's my favorite action game of the year so far, and you can read why in Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review. That explains why I think you should check the game out; Game Informer's list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks will get you some key information I wish I had when I started the game; and this guide I wrote up about the requirements you need to get the best ending in Phantom Blade Zero will help you find all story-critical content in the game.

However, you're looking for advice on which of the three visual modes Phantom Blade Zero offers you should use on your PS5. This here piece is for you.

Phantom Blade Zero has three visual modes on PS5 Pro: Quality, Balanced, and Performance. I tested all three. My personal favorite was Balanced, which gives you an upscaled (checkerboarded) 4K resolution at 40 FPS, as long as you have a 120Hz TV with VRR. If you have a 120Hz TV, it likely has VRR because most major manufacturers include it with 120Hz. I like this mode because the upscaled 4K looks beautiful, just a hair less than native 4K, and if you aren't someone super trained on those details, I'd wager you won't notice the difference. The best part is that this mode offers 40 FPS gameplay, which, contrary to how math works, is halfway between 30 FPS and 60 FPS; I'm not kidding, look it up. As such, 40 FPS feels much smoother than 30 FPS, and you're still getting crisp 4K resolution. It's a win-win for me and my go-to mode when a game offers it. That said, if you don’t have a PS5 Pro, you won’t see this Balanced mode.

The Performance mode offers an upscaled 2K resolution with a pretty locked 60 FPS. Phantom Blade Zero is an extremely fast, fluid action game, so I think many people will want the buttery smoothness of 60 FPS gameplay. If that's you, pick the Performance mode. Sure, its resolution is lower, and it will look blurrier and less crisp than the other two modes, but if you aren't switching back and forth often or looking at side-by-side images, you likely won't notice.

Quality mode is native 4K resolution (absolutely beautiful, the best visual image you can get playing Phantom Blade Zero), but at 30 FPS... and for a game like this, I don't think 30 FPS does it justice. I don't really recommend this mode for combat, but if you're just waltzing around Wulin, grabbing screenshots and such, turn it on and bask in the wonders of developer S-Game's art team. Note: There is an option for ray tracing on PS5 Pro. I tested all three graphics modes with it on and off and noticed zero performance changes or issues. So, use ray tracing – it’s nice!

And, in case you missed it, below is an image of the PC system requirements and specs needed to play Phantom Blade Zero on Steam and the Epic Games Store:

In the meantime, read Game Informer's Phantom Blade Zero review, then check out our list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks we wish we knew before starting the game. Then check out our breakdown of the requirements to see the best ending in the game.

#4239. The Duskbloods Delayed To 2027 So FromSoftware Can Adjust 'Game Rules And Balancing'

While the 2025 reveal of the Switch 2 came with many surprises, none were as unexpected as The Duskbloods. It's a Switch 2 exclusive, multiplayer-only title from FromSoftware, the developer behind games like Dark Souls and Elden Ring; in other words, not your typical Nintendo game. While The Duskbloods was originally scheduled to launch sometime this year, today the developer announced it's pushing the game's launch to 2027.

According to a post on The Duskbloods' X account, the main reason for the delay was balance-related. Here's the full statement:

While development of "The Duskbloods" is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027. We apologize to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support. During the network test, we saw active interest in the core concepts of the game, including combat, strategic depth, and player expression. To further enhance these aspects, we have decided to move the launch, allowing time for final adjustments to game rules and balancing.

We attended a hands-on preview session earlier this year and came away very positive, and sentiment was similar following the game's closed network test (that is, when the servers were working properly). It's not surprising that the devs have changes in mind following so much public feedback, though it is a little surprising that it will take until sometime next year for those adjustments to be complete.

To tide you over until the game's launch, check out our in-depth preview impressions or watch the video above to hear our live commentary over gameplay footage. You can also hear us discuss the game on our podcast, The Game Informer Show.

#4238. Nintendo Officially Rules Out Another Switch 2 Prince Increase

The Switch 2 launched for $449.99—now, it costs $499.99. But Nintendo isn't planning another price hike.

As reported by Reuters, the global memory shortage (often called the 'RAMpocalypse') spurred on by AI data centers has seen computing costs rise across the board, with next-gen consoles now looking at price tags of over $1,000.

However, according to Nintendo president Shuntaro Furukawa, the company has been able to secure enough memory to weather the shortage. As such, it is not currently considering future changes to the price.

Data centers are driving up prices because they require significant amounts of RAM, and manufacturers are now prioritizing AI companies over consumers.

That could, of course, change, but with the console already rising by $50 within its first year, rather than dropping as is typical with hardware, it's reassuring that Nintendo has hit pause for now.

As for rival console makers, Sony has also secured enough memory for the next fiscal year, which hopefully means that the PlayStation 5 won't face any further price hikes either. The PS5, for context, launched at $499.99 in 2020, but it now retails at $649.99, while the PS5 Pro is a staggering $899.99 in the US.

We're in the midst of a global memory shortage.

However, Xbox, which has seen enormous price hikes—the Series X now costs $799.99—has struggled to keep costs down despite working with suppliers to avoid another increase. The company says memory and storage have already risen more than 2.5 times, and expects them to double again by fall 2027.

"The entire consumer electronics industry is struggling with the current components crisis," Xbox said. "But the effects are particularly hard on consoles. Unlike phones, computers, speakers, and other consumer devices, consoles are typically not sold at a profit, but instead for less than they cost to make."

So, Nintendo and PlayStation appear to be done with price hikes for the fiscal year, while Xbox Series X/S consoles risk further increases. It doesn't mark the end of the global memory shortage, however, as next-gen consoles are still set for unprecedented price tags. But it's at least a reprieve from the unending news cycle of $50 bumps.

The Switch 2 is only a month old, and people already want to know how long it's going to be around.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

People seemingly haven't been able to stop playing Nioh 3 since the moment it came out, and everyone helped push the numbers to unprecedented heights for the series.

Nioh 3 has had a massive weekend on Steam, the type of launch you just don’t often see for Koei Tecmo games. Indeed, this has very clearly been a monumentous release for both the publisher, and developer Team Ninja.

It is also, quite visibly, the most popular Nioh release ever on PC, and it was impressive watching more and more players jump into the game over the weekend and push the numbers higher.

Nioh 3 came out swinging, breaking the series’ Steam concurrent player record immediately after lanch, with 42,822. Anyone keeping up with how well the game has been received, and how much it’s been anticipated by series fans and Soulslike players, would’ve told you that it was only the beginning.

Late on Friday, and several times on Saturday, the game continued achieving new records, setting new peak concurrent levels every couple of hours. It happened again on Sunday, when the game finally settled on its current 88,045 peak concurrent (via SteamDB).

That’s an incredibly healthy player base, but more than that, it’s more than double the previous record holder, Nioh 2, which peaked at 41,325 concurrent players in 2021. Steam players appear to be very happy with the game, too, with over 1,560 reviews and an overall Very Positive rating.

#4236. Assassin’s Creed Franchise Update Reveals Codename Hexe News Coming Next Year, New Game Plus for Valhalla, And Confirms No New Remakes

Ubisoft has released a fall update on the Assassin’s Creed franchise, providing news big and small on its flagship series. The news includes updates for existing games and smaller but significant insights on the various upcoming Assassin’s Creed games previously announced.

In terms of current games, Assassin’s Creed Valhalla is getting a long-requested New Game Plus thanks to a new update coming on November 5. This means you can start a fresh game while bringing over your progression items/level from your previous playthrough. This update will also introduce the following features:

This news comes a few days after New Game Plus arrived in Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

Codname Invictis, a PvP multiplayer game, remains in development as Ubisoft shares it has incorporated feedback from players who, according to Ubisoft, “saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed.” To this end, Ubisoft has spent months reworking Invictis to reflect this vague feedback and say the game is “now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions.”

As for the next single-player Assassin’s Creed, Codename Hexe, Ubisoft says it will share the next major update on this game in 2027. First announced in 2022, Codename Hexe is set during the 17th-century reign of the Holy Roman Empire, and the era's witch hunts will play a significant role.

With the release of Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced earlier this year, Ubisoft has given fans what they'll likely see as a disappointing update on potential future remakes: “One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development. Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories.”

However, Ubisoft adds that this door isn’t closed for good. “Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back,” says Ubisoft.

Ubisoft’s next update concerns the live-action Assassin's Creed series in production for Netflix. They say the show is “nearing completion” in Rome and that award-winning composer Hannah Peel (Insomnia, Rogue Agent, Game of Thrones: The Last Watch) is composing the score.

Lastly, Ubisoft teases big celebrations are planned for 2027, which marks the 20th anniversary of the Assassin's Creed franchise. It's keeping details to itself for now, but states it's "preparing a year of reveals, updates, rewards, and community moments. "

For more on Assassin's Creed, check out our review of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

#4235. Review: The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

You’re not ready for this. No matter how many trailers you’ve watched or how much pre-release footage you’ve pored over, walking out into Hyrule Field for the first time in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a revelatory experience.

It’s easy to forget how impactful Hyrule Field really was in the N64 original. While the game itself is still held in remarkably high regard, its main hub world has arguably been supplanted by later entries, particularly Breath of the Wild's enormous, immersive open world. It’s pioneering, yes, but it’s also quite small and empty when viewed through a modern lens.

The remake, with its breathtaking visuals, modernised controls, and revamped soundtrack, makes it feel new again. Standing at the entrance to Kokiri Forest and panning the camera around to soak in all of the details, I had to take a beat to stop myself being overcome by the enormity of the moment.

Making everything feel new again is really at the heart of the Switch 2 remake. I want to be clear: this is basically the same game, but Nintendo has tweaked just enough to make it feel fresh. Whether it’s the slightly different chest location for the Kokiri Sword or the Cucco hiding spots in Kakariko Village, there will always be something — however small — to give you pause.

The biggest change is the visuals. Much like Star Fox, Ocarina of Time is a staggering upgrade over the original, offering an almost overwhelming amount of detail across the board. From the small trinkets on Link’s tunic (who, by the way, is definitively 'Link' here, with no renaming options) to the way shards of broken pots stay on the ground and move underfoot, every aspect has been overhauled to take advantage of Switch 2’s power.

Yet despite the almost hyperrealistic visuals, it retains the original's spirit. There was a lot of discourse about the presentation when the remake was first properly revealed, particularly around characters’ faces. Any doubts about the approach will fade away as soon as you start playing. Everything looks right; whether it’s Link’s design or Zora's Domain, this is Ocarina of Time through and through. If you’re one of the many fans who were hoping to see the Spaceworld 2000 and Wii U tech demos properly realised, this is it and more.

The visual upgrades extend to the dungeons, of course, and it's crazy how impactful they are on your enjoyment. Inside the Deku Tree feels like a living world with realistic bark walls and copious spider webs. Likewise, the shimmering reflections and ethereal soundtrack completely transform the Water Temple. Despite minimal changes to the gameplay and structure — minor alterations to puzzles ultimately have little impact — the dungeons are a joy to explore once again.

It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. Assets in the distance — mountains and trees — look overly smooth and there’s some shimmering going on when you pan the camera around. It’s nowhere near as severe as Xenoblade Chronicles X on Switch 2, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice occasionally, particularly during handheld play.

Overall resolution takes a notable hit undocked, too, to the point where even Link himself can look a little fuzzy at times. It definitely needs mentioning, although it wasn't significantly detrimental to my experience. Keeping the game running smoothly feels like the more important priority, and Nintendo has nailed that aspect.

The audio has also been completely revamped, as well. The soundtrack, while familiar, has been reworked with new orchestral renditions, and everything from the Kokiri Forest track to the final, epic battle sounds incredible. Key cutscenes also feature voice acting, and it's some of the best I've heard from a first-party Nintendo game in quite some time. Your fairy companion Navi, whose in-game interruptions have been drastically cut down, is delightfully cheerful.

Exploring Hyrule and taking in the new visuals is made all the more satisfying thanks to the new control scheme. I’ve mentioned panning the camera around a couple of times, but it’s worth stressing that full camera control is completely new - a strange thing to highlight in 2026, but the ability to properly absorb everything this world has to offer really enhances your relationship with it. You feel so much more involved, and it helps that locations like Hyrule Castle Town have been upgraded to take advantage: no more pre-rendered backgrounds, you can now soak in all of the glorious detail.

The other major addition is the ability to jump whenever you please. Again, how quaint! Yet leaping at the press of a button gives you so much more autonomy over Link’s movements, even if it doesn’t open new routes or opportunities during your quest. You still jump at the same moments to scale platforms and solve puzzles, but doing it yourself without having to run off a ledge to trigger it is both quicker and more satisfying.

Combat feels comfortingly familiar: you lock onto your enemy and slash at them with ‘Y’, altering the direction of your swing by tilting the left analogue stick. You can hop about, perform a backwards somersault, and execute a leaping attack with either ‘X’ (the default jump button) or ‘A’, while holding and releasing ‘Y’ triggers the spin attack. It’s basically the same – why fix what isn’t broken, right?

Yet every attack now lands with such ferocity — accompanied by a searing red flash and a deafening crash — that combat feels completely overhauled. Again, old is new. Indeed, it’s so effective that it even makes Tears of the Kingdom's clashes feel comparatively tame.

Making use of your various weapons and items is also much easier than before. By holding down ‘R’, you’ll bring up an item inventory that instantly looks familiar if you’ve played TOTK or Echoes of Wisdom. Displayed in a single line, you quickly scroll left and right for your weapon of choice, whether it be a Deku Stick, a Bombchu, or the Megaton Hammer. The selection is relatively limited compared to, say, Echoes of Wisdom, so I never felt the UI was unwieldy or overwhelming; I always found what I was looking for straight away.

Meanwhile, key items like the Ocarina, masks, and Iron Boots are mapped to the D-pad. The latter is especially useful in the Water Temple, which gained its reputation as a major sticking point partly due to the need to repeatedly access the main menu to equip and unequip the boots. Tapping down on the D-pad is a lot more intuitive and makes for a breezier experience.

You can also do this for the newly-designed Lenses of Truth, which function exactly as the original Lens of Truth but have been revamped as a pair of goggles instead of a magnifying glass. It makes so much more sense!

The game is littered with similar tweaks, many of which have a noticeable quality-of-life impact. Reloading now drops you in the exact location you last saved (instead of at your house as Young Link and the Temple of Time as Adult Link). Elsewhere, the new Echo Gem, a reward from the House of Skulltula quest that replaces the Stone/Shard of Agony, shines and vibrates as you approach any Gold Skulltulas.

As for the Ocarina, you can play tunes in a variety of ways, the most basic of which is by simply pressing specific inputs via the face and shoulder buttons. Holding down ‘ZL’ brings up a menu of songs you’ve learned so far - handy for a quick reminder at any given moment.

However, you can also use the Switch 2’s built-in mic to input tunes using your own voice. Simply hum the tune you want and it’ll mostly pick it up with no fuss. You have the option to practice tunes if you wish, and it makes for a cute, if gimmicky way to use the Ocarina.

I’ve not been able to test Hori’s Electric Ocarina (and who knows where Nintendo’s official instrument is at), but I whipped out my guitar to test a few songs, and lo and behold, it actually worked. It certainly won’t be my go-to method, and chances are I’ll just stick to the buttons, but it’s neat.

I've not been able to test the Zelda Notes features during the review period, but you might find it a worthwhile addition if you're keen to create and share Ocarina songs. If you have some Zelda-themed amiibo lying about, tapping one during gameplay yields a few bonus items (arrows, recovery hearts, bombs, etc.), but thankfully nothing that could be deemed essential. All welcome additions, though.

What hasn’t been added for the remake is the Master Quest, and this is a real bummer. Available via a special GameCube release and as an unlockable in the 3DS remake, Master Quest proved an excellent way for veterans to test their skills upon completing the game. Given how closely the Switch 2 remake sticks to the core structure of the original, veterans will breeze through with minimal issues. And if you do ever get stuck, the new Threads of Time feature, which essentially documents your progress, will help you get back on track.

I died just once during the entire journey because I just got caught off-guard by an Iron Knuckle in the Spirit Temple. You can increase the difficulty slightly by altering the UI to show either minimal information or no information at all, but it’s no replacement for the changes that Master Quest could have brought. I'm hopeful that it will be added via an update, but it’s a glaring omission.

The lack of multiple save files is also disappointing. Yes, you can just create additional profiles at a system level, but the game allows you just one manual save along with several autosaves. Sometimes you just want to experience the start of the game again without impacting your main save file, so this is a shame.

The one last major addition is The Hall of Fallen Foes, and this is a cool, albeit inconsequential bonus. Accessed by sleeping in a bed after a specific campaign moment, here you can gaze upon statues based on enemies you’ve slain. It’s a lovely way to properly appreciate their updated designs, and you’re also given the opportunity to replay boss fights or even take on multiple bosses in succession. The rewards for doing so are useless, but the act of optimising your battles and beating your time is fun enough on its own.

And so, even with all that knowledge, you're really not ready for this. The visuals, the gameplay, the audio – everything has been thoughtfully upgraded to such a degree that this will completely replace the original for many. While the lack of Master Quest means it falls short of being definitive, it's still a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2.

Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time.

That said, it is a very safe remake. Despite lots of minor changes throughout, it’s still essentially the same game you’ve likely already played, and so you might find it offers little challenge if you’re familiar with the N64 original or 3DS remake. This makes the lack of Master Quest — or really any kind of hard mode — particularly glaring, but I’m hopeful it’ll be added in the future.

You fight an awful lot in this game, it doesn't need to feel like an explosion every sword strike. The score is pretty but a bit overcooked in spots, though that's also typical of the modern day. Subtlety is a premium, everything has to be glammed up. It's like an overcorrection for the excessive drabness.

There's no hero mode either. A remake should have at least a hook or two to get the original players a little excited. But they did a cool job of importing some continuity from recent titles and of course they couldn't stray much from the source on a title this beloved, where gamers lose their mind over a 9/10.

Just want to point out that I feel pretty confident that we would have possibly the same level of vitriole (maybe from the other side of the argument?) if this score had been a 10/10. It feels like every time this site or IGN releases a perfect score, they are criticized for being corporate shills, Nintendoters, lazy reviewers, etc. So, let's please be respectful and kind, take a couple breaths, and try to have some perspective. I know it can be frustrating to feel like your favorite/beloved [blank] isn't getting the appreciation or glory or credibility you feel it deserves - I was hoping for a 10 here, too! - but it doesn't have to take anything away from the enjoyment of it. I guarantee you are not alone with your love and passion for these media. But let's also try to understand that we - the people writing these reviews, included - are all individuals with subjective points-of-view. Everyone else's opinions are just as valid as your own. Share away, but can't we keep it reasonable and tolerant? Please. Hope everyone that wants to gets to enjoy their time with this game! Looking forward to playing it myself, tomorrow! 🕊🌈

Assets in the distance — mountains and trees — look overly smooth and there’s some shimmering going on when you pan the camera around. It’s nowhere near as severe as Xenoblade Chronicles X on Switch 2, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice occasionally, particularly during handheld play.

Overall resolution takes a notable hit undocked, too, to the point where even Link himself can look a little fuzzy at times. It definitely needs mentioning, although it wasn't significantly detrimental to my experience. Keeping the game running smoothly feels like the more important priority, and Nintendo has nailed that aspect."

#4234. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

#4233. Love and Deepspace ushers in the Year of the Horse with a Wuxia-inspired AU multi-banner and a restaurant management mini-game

A new Love and Deepspace banner event is here with a lot of rewards to earn, and brand-new Memories for all five lads to unlock.

Love and Deepspace has kicked off the next big in-game moment and is celebrating Chinese New Year with the arrival of a new 5-Star Memory Series. This year's spring-themed banner is available now until February 27, and it comes with a host of events.

The Mortality’s Tenderness banner features five new limited-time 5-Star Memories, one each for the game’s five love interests. The theme is all about warmth, reunion, and intimacy, taking place in a Wuxia-inspired setting that's once again an alternate universe from the main story of the game.

The new memory cards are Xavier: Blades with Blossoms, Zayne: Entwined Kites, Rafayel: Carved Gemheart, Sylus: Shared Lanterns, and Caleb: Clearday Return. You can pick three of the five to focus on and further pick one to guarantee on your second 5-star pull; and you can earn wish rewards by making cumulative wishes over the course of the event.

Some of the rewards you could get include limited headwear, Limited Deepspace Wishes, and — of course — Memory-themed outfits and hairstyles inspired by the new Memories. Outside of wish rewards, the Memory Series comes with growth tasks that rewards you with in-game materials for levelling up the new cards during the event. When you reach Rank 1 for any new Memory from the banner, you’ll earn a Memory-themed outfit with a special colour that matches your chosen love interest.

Illusio returns as part of the new event, too, letting you customise the look of Kindled Moments across all five new Memories. Things you can customise include selecting the outfits and accessories for each love interest, so you can recreate Kindled Moments in your own style. As always, Kindled Moments will go back to their default look after the event ends.

There’s a new mini-game to play, too, available only during the event. It’s called Courteous Fare, a frantic but familiar restaurant management simulation that allows you to unlock a variety of rewards.

Furthermore, if you log in for 10 days throughout the event, you can unlock a new outfit set, Wealth Overflow, which can be worn by any of the love interests as well as the heroine. There are other login rewards, too, like 10 Deepspace Wishes, 10 Empyrean Wishes, His and My Outfit sets, two dynamic portrait photo poses, and loads more.

Finally, the Golden Fortune event adds even more daily log in rewards in the form of one free "shake" per day, from which you can earn a random reward of between 68 and 108 Diamonds — that adds up to a total of 1,296 Diamonds if you show up every day.

#4232. Sir Patrick Stewart, Star Trek, X-Men, And Myriad Video Games Actor, Passes Away

According to a report from The Hollywood Reporter, actor Sir Patrick Stewart has passed away at the age of 86. Stewart spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, shared that he died after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.”

Stewart was best known for his roles as Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation (and its various spinoffs) and Charles Xavier in the X-Men films, but he did plenty of video game performing, too. Stewart played Emperor Uriel Septim VII in The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion, one of the first characters you meet in the game, and Zobek in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow. He also played Jean-Luc Picard in about 10 different Star Trek games and Charles Xavier in five different X-Men games.

Stewart will always be a crucial voice and face in the legacy of sci-fi entertainment. Jean-Luc Picard will undoubtedly be an enduring and important character in the Star Trek franchise, and that's thanks to Stewart's portrayal of the starship captain. His portrayal of Charles Xavier also helped to legitimize the comic book movie, and he will appear again as the character in this year's upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.

Our thoughts are with his friends and family, and the millions of fans (of which I include myself) who are mourning his loss. Let's all drink some Earl Grey tea in his honor today.

#4231. Brooklyn's First GTA 6 Mural Has Been Vandalised After Less Than A Month

Brooklyn’s first Grand Theft Auto 6 mural, which took the artist seven whole days to paint by hand, has been tagged by a graffiti artist who’s getting a ton of heat from fans.

To say that GTA 6’s marketing cycle has been strange would be an understatement. After fans spent literal years begging for just a smidgen of news while Rockstar kept quiet and locked itself away to work on the world’s most anticipated game, things very quickly changed over the past two months.

What was once deafening silence, moon theories, and digging through trailers turned into a massive gameplay deep dive, magazine covers, exclusive controllers, a whole soundtrack album, new trailers, and a bunch of artwork. Like with GTA 5, some of that artwork has even appeared in the real world, leaving it open to getting ruined, like what just happened in Brooklyn.

As pointed out by Redditor BrendalBallentine on the GTA subreddit, Brooklyn’s massive hand-painted mural of the GTA 6 launch trailer artwork has recently been defaced by a graffiti artist called “jelous”, who put their tag at the bottom of the piece. The artist then decided to share what they’d done on their public Instagram page, catching the attention of the GTA community.

Sony is right - Grand Theft Auto 6 is probably going to play best on PlayStation.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the reactions to the defacing have not been positive, with many jumping into jelous’ comments to call him out and even leading him to turn them off altogether. Of course, there are also plenty making fun of the “leave the billion-dollar company alone” vibes that some are giving, but I think I’m mostly with the fans on this one.

One fan on Reddit pointed out that tagging a mural advertising a game about crime is almost poetic, but then gets cancelled out by taking a picture and sharing it on social media.

While, yes, the mural is marketing at the end of the day, it’s also something that an artist painted by hand for seven days, which is no easy task considering how massive it is. GTA games also don’t exactly come around often, so there’s a bit of reverence for these murals and real-world marketing that makes a frankly uninteresting tag a lame addition.

I don’t think Rockstar and Take-Two are going to be rushing down to the mural like some GTA fans are hoping for in the comments, but it is a bit of a shame to see such a nice piece vandalised. At least there’s so much GTA 6 marketing now that you don’t have to go too far to see something else to do with the game.

#4230. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4229. Death Stranding Isolations Animated Series Gets New Teaser Trailer

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. Isolations is created by Japanese animation studio E&H Production (Ninja Kamui, Bullet/Bullet, Magic Knight Rayerath) and directed by Takayuki Sano.  Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima serves as executive producer.

Today’s teaser video provides the following story synopsis:

The Death Stranding—a catastrophic series of explosions caused when the dead crept into our world and collided with the living.

In the wake of this cataclysm, many were forced to live in absolute isolation—among them, a young girl. Although this lonely existence was forced upon her, she soon grows to prefer solitude, eschewing all opportunities for real human connection and allowing herself to be strung along by fate.

In Death Stranding, legendary game creator Hideo Kojima brought you a haunting vision of a shattered world. Now, that world expands into new frontiers with a brand-new animation series.

Under the guidance of director Takayuki Sano, world-class hand-drawn animations have been brought to life by renowned studio “E&H production” (NINJA KAMUI, BULLET/BULLET, the Magic Knight Rayearth television series).

The story is set in North America immediately after Sam—the protagonist of the game—reconnects the continent by means of the Chiral Network. However, as America is reborn from the ashes, the renewed connections that bind it together bring about new and unforeseen consequences.

In this tumultuous new landscape, there are some who walk a different path to the one chosen by Sam and his Bridges comrades: a wise old man who connects people through a method that defies all reckoning; a female soldier ensnared in a cycle of war and destruction; a boy who seethes with rage at the absurdity of his life...and of course, the girl who chose to sever all ties with the outside world...Fate has other plans for her, however, and chance encounters see her launched headfirst into a world she does not recognize.

Death Stranding Isolations is coming to Disney+ and Hulu in 2027. It’s one of the three planned big-screen adaptations of the series. An animated movie called Death Stranding: Mosquito (working title) is also in the works alongside a live-action Death Stranding film by A24.

For more on Death Stranding, check out our reviews for the first game and its 2025 sequel. You can also read the latest update on Kojima Productions’ upcoming stealth-espionage game, Physint.
